sens: Physical space that extends broadly, without obstacles or constraints
Freedom of movement, absence of oppression
Situation of relief or deliverance after a trial
H4800.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a spacious place, an area that opens widely before one: a plain, an open space. In Hosea 4:16, Israel is compared to a lamb that grazes "in wide pastures" — the image is of an animal that can move freely in an unbounded landscape.

2. Figuratively, "wide" expresses freedom of movement and the absence of constraint. When the psalmist says, "You will set my feet in a wide place" (Psalms 31:9), he is asking God to free him from his enemies and oppression: it is moving from a narrow, suffocating space to a free space where one can breathe.

3. The word finally takes on a spiritual significance: being set "wide" means being delivered from distress or danger. In Psalms 118:5, the psalmist cries, "Out of my distress I called on the Lord" and testifies that "the Lord set me in a wide place" — deliverance is perceived as a transition from narrowness to expansion, from suffering to freedom.
H4800.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to widen, to become spacious." It is related to other terms describing openness, expansion, and freedom. The initial image is always physical and concrete: a place without walls or boundaries, an open horizon. This is why the Bible often uses it to speak of God's deliverance or help, which frees the oppressed as one brings someone out of a confined place.
H4800.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and the historical Pentateuch. Its usage is almost always figurative and spiritual: it describes God's saving action. In 2 Samuel 22:20 and Psalms 18:20 (which are the same psalm), David testifies that God "set him in a wide place" and saved him. This association between being set wide and divine help recurs in Psalms 31:9 and 118:5. Only Hosea 4:16 and Habakkuk 1:6 use the word in a more literal sense to describe geographical spaces (plains, expanses of land). Each time, the underlying idea is that of liberation or unimpeded movement.
H4800.portee: This word reminds us that God's deliverance is not an abstract notion, but a concrete experience: moving from narrowness to expansion, from suffocation to free breathing. For the Christian who suffers or feels oppressed, "being set wide" evokes the powerful action of God that breaks chains and restores freedom. It is a promise that distress is not definitive, and that God is capable of transforming the situation — bringing us from a confined place to an open horizon.

sens: That is at a great distance in space
That comes from a distant place
That extends over a vast area
That is figuratively removed, rejected
H4801.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning designates what is separated from us by a great distance: one thinks of a place that requires time and effort to reach. When Jeremiah announces that the Lord will bring "a nation from afar against you" (Jeremiah 5:15), he evokes an enemy power coming from very far away.

2. The adjective also qualifies what comes from a distant region, what comes from the ends of the earth. The virtuous woman in Proverbs 31:14 "brings her food from afar," meaning she obtains her goods through exchanges or trade from far-off lands.

3. The word can also describe a vast expanse: in Isaiah 33:17, the eyes "will behold the land in all its breadth," a spatial dimension that is both wide and deep.

4. Figuratively, it expresses distance or separation: Psalm 138:6 speaks of one who "is high and lifted up" and "sees from afar," meaning he looks from above, establishing a distance that marks divine superiority and judgment.
H4801.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be distant, to move away." It expresses the fundamental idea of separation in space and, by extension, relative distance to an observer or point of reference. The root is also found in Aramaic with a similar meaning. The word opposes what is near, immediate, or current.
H4801.emploi: This word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs). It primarily describes distant places — far-off nations, lands seen from the sky — or objects brought from afar. The prophetic context dominates: the distance of the nations that God brings back or uses to strike. It is a very concrete and geographical notion, but also an image of divine sovereignty, which sees and acts "from afar" on human affairs.
H4801.portee: This word reminds the believing reader that God is not limited by distance. His gaze penetrates the most distant lands, and His power reaches the powers that seem too far away to be touched. It also invites trust: the one who governs distant nations and brings back exiles from afar is the faithful shepherd of His people.

sens: cooking utensil for frying or grilling food
shallow container intended for cooking over fire
H4802.detail: 1. It is a cooking utensil, a shallow pan or grill, used to cook or prepare food over fire. In Leviticus 2:7, it speaks of a "gift cooked on the grill," which shows that cakes made from flour kneaded with oil are cooked directly in contact with fire or heat. 2. More broadly, it is a cooking container used to prepare dishes in the context of sacrifices offered to God. In Leviticus 7:9, "the offering baked in the oven, prepared on the grill or in the pan" refers to different ways of preparing the sacrifice: this word thus covers both oven cooking, grilling, and frying, all flat or shallow utensils for cooking.
H4802.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning probably "to dig" or "to scrape," which evokes a hollow and shallow container shaped or crafted for cooking. This root appears in other words related to cooking or cooking utensils. The basic image is that of a shaped, hollow object used to prepare food.
H4802.emploi: The word appears twice in the Law of Moses, always in the context of offerings and sacrifices to the Lord (Leviticus 2:7 and 7:9). It designates the utensil on which certain grain offerings (cakes of flour) are prepared, which can be cooked in several ways: in the oven, on the grill, or in the pan. It is a term strictly related to worship and the preparation of sacred dishes, never used for ordinary cooking in the preserved biblical texts.
H4802.portee: This word reminds us that the worship rendered to God involved all daily gestures, even the simplest like cooking. Offerings are not abstract gifts: it is bread, prepared with care, cooked in the pan or oven, offered to the Lord. This shows that God is interested in our concrete actions, in what we offer Him with our hands, and that even cooking can be an act of worship and devotion.

sens: Remove hair, make bald or hairless
Make smooth and shiny by rubbing
Prepare a weapon for battle by sharpening and polishing
Quality of being strong, robust, vigorous
H4803.detail:
1. Remove hair: this means to make someone bald or hairless. In Leviticus 13:40, the priest examines a man whose head is "devoid of hair": this is a sign that his skin is diseased but that the man is clean according to the Law. It is also an act of humiliation or mourning: in Nehemiah 13:25, Nehemiah "pulls out the hair" of men who have transgressed the covenant, showing his anger and disapproval.
2. Make smooth and shiny: this means to polish an object by rubbing it to give it a beautiful surface. In 1 Kings 7:45, all the bronze utensils made for the Temple by King Solomon are "polished", meaning they are worked and shiny, worthy of divine worship.
3. Sharpen and prepare a sword: this means to make it sharp and shiny for battle. In Ezekiel 21:14-16, God speaks of His sword of judgment: it is "sharpened" and "polished", ready to strike. This verb shows that the weapon is meticulously prepared, formidable.
4. Quality of strength and vigor: sometimes the word refers to physical robustness. In Isaiah 18:7, a people is described as "strong and vigorous", capable of bringing offerings to God.
H4803.origine: The Hebrew verb מָרַט (maraṭ) comes from a root that evokes the action of rubbing, smoothing, removing. The same root produces words related to nudity and baldness, as stripping something is to make it bare or smooth. The basic image is that of the hand's action that removes or polishes: removing hair by rubbing hard, polishing a metal object by working it continuously.
H4803.emploi: The verb מָרַט appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in prophetic poetry and legal texts. In Leviticus (chapters 13-14), it describes baldness as a visible sign in the diagnosis of leprosy: a bald man can be clean if his skin has no other defect. In 1 Kings 7, it characterizes the meticulous work of Solomon's workers in the Temple: the objects of worship must be polished, perfect, reflecting God's majesty. In the prophets (especially Ezekiel 21 and Isaiah 50), the verb becomes a warrior or judgmental image: God's sword is sharpened and polished, terrible and ready. In Nehemiah 13, the brutal act of pulling out hair is an act of punishment and mourning in the face of unfaithfulness. The word thus changes context: natural or ritual action in Leviticus, artistic work in 1 Kings, image of divine judgment in the prophets, act of anger in Nehemiah.
H4803.portee: This word teaches that a weapon or object prepared with care becomes terrible or magnificent: the Bible compares God's judgment to a sharpened and polished sword, showing that God's anger is not disorderly but precise and inevitable. It also shows that even acts of mourning or humiliation (pulling out hair) are means that God allows to remind His people of the seriousness of unfaithfulness. For the reader, it is an invitation to take divine words seriously: they are prepared, sharp, effective.

sens: Brutally remove something attached to something else
Remove feathers or hair from an animal
In a figurative sense: to take away, remove, strip
H4804.detail:
1. To tear out means to remove something by pulling forcefully: this is what happens to the wings of the young eagle in Daniel 7:4, where they are taken from the body of the beast.
2. By extension, the verb is used to refer to removing the feathers or hair covering an animal — a rough action that denudes.
3. The image extends figuratively to express any brutal removal, anything that deprives or strips: tearing someone from their power, position, or strength.
H4804.origine: The Hebrew verb מְרַט comes from a root that evokes the idea of pulling, removing by force. It is related to other Hebrew verbs expressing the action of removing or tearing. The basic image is physical and concrete: that of the gesture of someone pulling to detach.
H4804.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 7:4, in the vision of the four beasts. The wings of the first beast (a lion with eagle's wings) are torn off, symbolizing the loss of its power and greatness. This apocalyptic context emphasizes the violent and definitive nature of the action: what is torn away does not return.
H4804.portee: This word reminds the believer that God controls history and can remove power from the world's powers. The torn wings signify that no one can indefinitely retain their strength without Him; it is an invitation not to rely on human empires, but on Him who judges them.

sens: Action of revolting against authority
One who refuses to obey
Character of one who systematically refuses to listen and submit
H4805H.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses the act of revolting, openly refusing established authority: it is an active and conscious disobedience. Nehemiah 9:17 illustrates this well when it describes the people who "in their rebellion, appointed a leader to return to their slavery"—an open revolt against God and His plan.
2. It then designates the person who revolts, the rebel himself: someone who refuses to submit to God or His representative. Ezekiel 3:26 speaks of "a family of rebels" to describe the people Ezekiel must confront without being able to correct them.
3. It is also the character trait of one who systematically refuses to listen to God's voice. Isaiah 30:9 shows this: "it is a rebellious people, they are lying children, children who do not want to listen to the law of the Lord"—an attitude of persistent opposition to the divine message.
H4805H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to be bitter, sour", from which it has shifted to mean "to be in disagreement" and ultimately "to revolt". This image of bitterness well reflects the tension and hostility: a rebel has a bitter heart against the one who commands him. Rebellion stands diametrically opposed to obedience, which is the central attitude of biblical faith.
H4805H.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophets Ezekiel (14 occurrences) and Nehemiah, as well as Isaiah. It regularly describes the attitude of the people of Israel or Judah towards God and His prophets. Sometimes it refers to the act of revolting (Numbers 17:10, Deuteronomy 31:27), sometimes to the rebellious person (Ezekiel 2:7, Ezekiel 3:26), but always in a religious context: it is rebellion against God or against a man speaking in God's name. The word never softens: it retains the force to denote a serious breach of the covenant.
H4805H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word sheds light on the seriousness of disobedience towards God. The Bible does not view rebellion as a mere deviation, a weakness: it is a revolt, a hostile choice that breaks the filial relationship with God. At the same time, the rebellion of the Israelites remains an occasion for divine mercy (Nehemiah 9:17 shows this), reminding us that the forgiveness offered by God is greater than our revolt.

sens: Young beef cattle fed and fattened for slaughter or sacrifice
Animal offered in sacrifice or at a solemn feast
Wealth and abundance
Well-being and prosperity
H4806.detail:
1. A fat calf is a young bull that has been generously fed to make it tasty and meaty. It is the animal chosen for important meals. Adonijah sacrifices one to celebrate his accession to the throne (1 Kings 1:9), and David offers one during the solemn installation of the ark (2 Samuel 6:13).
2. In religious ceremonies, the fat calf is among the offerings made to God. But the prophet Isaiah reminds us that these sacrifices of fattened animals are worthless without the justice of the heart: "I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fed beasts" (Isaiah 1:11).
3. This word evokes wealth and material abundance. One who possesses fat calves possesses goods, well-fed livestock, and thus prosperity. This is why royal feasts center around them: they are the dishes of the powerful.
4. The fat calf symbolizes well-being and carnal satisfaction. In the picture of messianic peace (Isaiah 11:6), the animals that are fattened live in harmony, imagery of a world finally reconciled.
H4806.origine: The Hebrew word derives from a root meaning "to fatten" or "to prosper." The same verb, used in the passive form, means "to be fat" or "to be nourished." This family is found in contexts of food abundance and livestock fattening. The word properly designates the result: the animal made fat by the care it receives.
H4806.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly during important feasts. In 1 Kings 1:9, 1:19, and 1:25, Adonijah sacrifices fat calves to celebrate a royal inauguration banquet: it marks the solemnity and lordly expense. David also offers one during a major religious ceremony (2 Samuel 6:13). Isaiah mentions them twice: once to criticize blind trust in animal sacrifices (1:11), and once in a vision of peace where the fattened animals live without threat (11:6). The word is thus concentrated in scenes where it embodies either power and feasting or prophetic criticism of religious formalism.
H4806.portee: The fat calf reminds us that our God is not blind to our way of living or our priorities. Sacrificing fat calves to gods or fattening animals while ignoring social justice reveals a loss of values: it is the heart that matters, not the spectacular material abundance. But the fat calf also evokes that God ordains good physical life: there is nothing shameful about eating well, if it is accompanied by righteousness and generosity.

sens: son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul
another name for Mephibosheth
H4807.detail: Merib-Baal is a man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Prince Jonathan (son of King Saul) and appears in the genealogies of the book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40), where he is presented as the father of Micah. Merib-Baal is a second name given to the same person called elsewhere Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4), probably because the name changed over time or for religious reasons related to the worship of Baal.
H4807.origine: The name Merib-Baal literally means "Baal is my advocate" or "Baal is my master," composed of "merib" (contention, master) and "Baal" (the false god worshiped in Canaan). This name belongs to a period when the Israelite royal family still bore names mentioning the god Baal, before Israel's religious reform rejected this worship. The name change to Mephibosheth likely reflects an intentional correction of the textual tradition.
H4807.emploi: Merib-Baal appears twice in the biblical text, in the two identical passages of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 8:34 and 9:40), which reproduce the genealogy of the house of Saul. In these two verses, he is designated as the son of Jonathan and the father of Micah. He is the same person as Mephibosheth, mentioned several times in 2 Samuel with more details about his life and his relationship with King David, but in Chronicles, the text exclusively uses the name Merib-Baal.

sens: Disagreement, quarrel between two people or two groups
Rebellion, refusal to obey against the authority of God
H4808.detail:
1. The word designates a confrontation, a quarrel between people. When Abraham says to Lot, "Let there be no dispute between me and you," he speaks of the tension that threatens to divide their families and flocks (Genesis 13:8). It is a conflict that arises from disagreement or jealousy.
2. The word takes on a more serious tone when it designates a revolt against God. In Numbers 27:14, the "desert of Zin" is the very place where the Israelites contested the authority of Moses and that of God — which is why it is called the "waters of contention." This dispute is not a mere disagreement: it is a refusal to obey.
H4808.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to contest," "to oppose." It is from the same family as other Hebrew words that express conflict and tension. The Greek of the New Testament often translates this reality with words from the same field, which designate both a human quarrel and an opposition to God.
H4808.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence, in Genesis 13:8, places it at the heart of a family scene: Abraham seeks to prevent it by allowing Lot to choose his land first. The second, in Numbers 27:14, links it to a foundational event in Israel's history, the incident of the "waters of Meribah" (Kadesh), where the rebellious people contested Moses. This place becomes emblematic of unfaithfulness: it bears the very name of the dispute.
H4808.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that conflict takes very different forms. Among believers, it is a matter of humility and forgiveness: Abraham prefers peace to his right. With God, it is infinitely more serious: contesting His order is rebellion. The lesson is clear: avoid disputes with brothers, and never contest the Word of God.

sens: Water source in the desert of Sinai, at Rephidim
Water source at Kadesh, in the southern part of the promised land
Symbol of the rebellion and contestation of the people against God
H4809G.detail:
1. Meribah is primarily a real fountain, located at Rephidim in the desert of Sinai (Exodus 17:7). It is there that the Israelites, thirsty during their exodus from Egypt, complained against Moses and against God, questioning the divine presence among them.
2. The same name also designates a water source at Kadesh, on the southern border of the promised land, where the people again protested against God and against Moses (Deuteronomy 33:8). These two places bear the same name because the same events occurred there: the thirst of the Israelites and their lack of trust.
3. Meribah becomes a spiritual symbol of rebellion, contestation, and refusal to trust God despite His past miracles. The psalmist invokes it as a warning: do not harden your heart as "in Meribah" (Psalms 95:8), meaning do not imitate that generation that doubted.
H4809G.origine: The name Meribah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "contention," "quarrel," or "dispute." It recalls the verb that describes the Israelites' contestation: they "contested" against God and against Moses. The place received this name as a memorial of this negative event, a lasting trace of the people's lack of faith.
H4809G.emploi: Meribah appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. First in Exodus 17:7, where Moses names the place after the people murmured against him and God because of thirst. Then in Deuteronomy 33:8, where Moses recalls that God "tested" Levi at Massah and "contended" with him at Meribah — trials that purified the Levitical tribe. Finally, in Psalms 95:8, where the psalmist exhorts not to reproduce the unbelief of Meribah and Massah. These three uses inscribe Meribah in the memory of the people as a moment when faith wavered.
H4809G.portee: Meribah reminds believers that unbelief and contestation of God leave lasting marks. It is a warning: having seen God's miracles (the exodus from Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea) does not prevent the temptation to doubt when trials arise. The name invites us to remain confident in God's faithfulness, even in difficult moments.

sens: A water source in the desert of Sinai, near Rephidim
Another water source at Kadesh, on the southern border of the promised land
The place where Israel rebelled against God by demanding water
An act of disobedience and contention against God
H4809H.detail:
1. Meriba primarily refers to a fountain located at Rephidim, in the desert of Sinai, which provided water to the Israelites during their exodus from Egypt. It is a specific water point, geographically identifiable.
2. The name Meriba also applies to a water source at Kadesh, which is located on the southern border of the territory that God promises to the children of Israel. Like at Rephidim, it is a concrete place, a source that people could see and recognize.
3. These two places bear the same name because the people contended with God at both sources: they murmured, complained, and demanded water, doubting the goodness and power of the Lord (Numbers 20:13: "where the children of Israel contended with the Lord").
4. Meriba thus comes to symbolize the rebellion and unbelief of the chosen people: it has become the name of disobedience itself, not just of a place (Psalms 106:32: "They provoked the Lord near the waters of Meriba").
H4809H.origine: The name Meriba comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to contend" or "to dispute" — it signifies a confrontation, a quarrel. The word expresses the idea of a contention, a claim against someone. Here, the name of the place carries all the drama: it is not simply a source, it is the place where Israel contended with God face to face, hence its significant name.
H4809H.emploi: Meriba appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in four key passages. Moses and Aaron were severely judged there: at Kadesh, Meriba, instead of trusting the Lord, Moses struck the rock at the command of the people rather than speaking to it, which cost them entry into the Promised Land (Numbers 20:24; Deuteronomy 32:51). Psalm 81 refers to Meriba as a moment of testing where God tested His people (Psalms 81:8). Psalm 106 recalls that Israel's irritation at Meriba provoked the Lord's anger and serious consequences (Psalms 106:32). Ezekiel uses Meriba as a geographical landmark to delineate the restored promised land (Ezekiel 47:19).
H4809H.portee: Meriba is a lasting warning in the memory of Israel: it is the name of an act of doubt that closed the door to the great leaders of the people. For the believer, this name reminds us that incessant demands and unbelief in the face of difficulties can break trust in God. It is also a call to respect God's authority and to believe in His providence, even when circumstances seem desperate.

sens: Son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul
Alternate name of King Mephibosheth
H4810.detail:
1. Merib-Baal is a man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Prince Jonathan (who is himself the son of King Saul) and the father of Michah. In 1 Chronicles 9:40, he is presented as an ancestor in the genealogy of Benjamin, indicating his importance in the royal family history.

2. Merib-Baal is another name given to Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan. This character bears two names in the biblical texts: "Merib-Baal" (meaning "Baal is my advocate") and "Mephibosheth." These two names refer to the same person, and different books of the Bible use one or the other depending on the passages.
H4810.origine: The name "Merib-Baal" literally means "Baal is my advocate" or "Baal is my dispute." It consists of two elements: "merib" (dispute, contention) and "Baal" (lord, master). This name reflects a common practice among ancient Israelites of the royal period, who incorporated the name of the god Baal into proper names. The character is also called "Mephibosheth" (likely meaning "the one who dissolves shame"), with this latter name becoming predominant in later narratives.
H4810.emploi: Merib-Baal appears in the genealogy of Benjamin preserved in 1 Chronicles. Son of Prince Jonathan and grandson of King Saul, he represents the royal lineage that survived after the fall of the house of Saul. Although this character is an important historical figure for royal succession, the Bible mainly mentions him through his genealogy: he is presented as the father of Michah and as a link in the chain of generations of Benjamin. The same man is elsewhere called Mephibosheth, showing how proper names could vary in the transmission of biblical texts.

sens: Priest during the Exile and Return, head of a priestly family
H4811.detail: Meraja is a Jewish priest who appears in the genealogical lists of the return from Exile, during the time of the high priest Jehoiakim. His name is listed among the heads of priestly families, indicating that he led a lineage of priests and had significant responsibilities in the service of the restored temple (Nehemiah 12:12).
H4811.origine: The name Meraja means "rebellion" in Hebrew, formed from the root that evokes revolt or insubordination. It is a rather rare name in the Old Testament, and it is found only with this single character. The etymology suggests that the name could evoke a protest or an assertion of independence, although the biblical context gives no indication of why this name was chosen for this man.
H4811.emploi: Meraja appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:12. This passage lists the priests and heads of priestly families who served under the high priest Jehoiakim, upon the return from Exile to Jerusalem. His name is mentioned as the head of the priestly house of Seraja, indicating that he held a position of responsibility in the hierarchy of the restored worship. It is a simple name in a list, without any particular story or anecdote concerning this priest.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Levi living during the time of the Divided Monarchy
Priestly ancestor of the lineage of Eleazar son of Aaron
Head of a priestly house
H4812G.detail:
1. Merajoth is the name of a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy in Israel. He belongs to one of the great priestly families descended from Eleazar, the son of Aaron.
2. Merajoth appears as a key priestly ancestor: he is the son of Zechariah and the father of Amaria (1 Chronicles 6:6-7), placing him in the direct genealogy of the high priests. He is certified to descend from Eleazar, granting him a legitimate place in the priesthood.
3. Several men bear this name across different generations, all heads of priestly houses. The text mentions at least three: one of the ancestors of the high priest Seraja (Nehemiah 11:11), and a representative of a priestly family during the time of Jehoiakim (after the exile).
H4812G.origine: The name Merajoth means "rebel" in Hebrew, formed from a root evoking rebellion or resistance. Although the meaning of the name is negative, the men who bear it are faithful priests, indicating that the name likely did not determine character. This name appears exclusively in the priestly genealogies of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah.
H4812G.emploi: Merajoth is mentioned six times in the Old Testament, solely in the genealogical lists of the return from exile and the Levitical genealogies. In 1 Chronicles 6:6-7, he appears in the lineage of the priests, sons of Aaron. He reappears in 1 Chronicles 9:11 and Nehemiah 11:11 as an ancestor of the high priest Seraja (or Seraiah) who lived after the return from Babylon. In Ezra 7:3, he is listed in the genealogy of the scribe Ezra himself. These repetitions highlight the genealogical importance of this priestly family in establishing the legitimacy of the priests returned from exile.

sens: Priest of Judah at the time of the return from exile
H4812H.detail: 1. Merajoth is a Jewish priest who lived at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile. He was the head of a family of priests and was represented by his son Helkai during the drafting of the list of priests and Levites under the governance of the high priest Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:15).
H4812H.origine: The name means "rebellious" or "one who revolts." It appears in the genealogy of priests who descended from Eleazar, son of Aaron, and formed an important branch of the post-exilic Jewish clergy. It is a name borne by several members of this priestly lineage.
H4812H.emploi: Merajoth appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:15, in a passage listing the heads of families of priests and Levites at the time of the temple restoration. This context shows that the priests were reorganizing their service and hierarchy after the return from Babylon. The text notes that Merajoth was represented by his son Helkai in this official list.

sens: Elder sister of Moses and Aaron
Prophetess in the desert
Woman of the tribe of Levi during the time of Egypt and the Exodus
H4813G.detail:
1. Mary was the elder sister of Moses and Aaron, all three children of Amram and Jochebed, from the tribe of Levi. She played a decisive role at the time of the Exodus: it was she who watched over baby Moses when he was placed in a basket by the Nile until Pharaoh's daughter discovered him.
2. Mary is presented as a prophetess: after the crossing of the Red Sea, she took a tambourine and danced in front of the women of Israel, singing God's victory. The text specifically says, "Mary, the prophetess, sister of Aaron" (Exodus 15:20), confirming her role as a spokesperson for the Lord.
3. In Numbers 12, Mary and Aaron contradict Moses because of his marriage to a Cushite woman. God intervenes to defend Moses and punishes Mary with leprosy that covers her for seven days; the people wait for her recovery before resuming their journey.
H4813G.origine: The name "Miriam" literally means "rebellion" in Hebrew, but this meaning should not diminish the character: it rather expresses the intensity or strength of character. Mary is mentioned in several books (Exodus, Numbers, 1 Chronicles, Deuteronomy, Micah), which shows the importance of her memory in Israel.
H4813G.emploi: Mary appears as a major figure in the story of the Exodus. Exodus 15:20-21 shows her celebrating the deliverance from the Red Sea with the women of Israel. Numbers 12 recounts her conflict with Moses: she and Aaron contradict his authority regarding his marriage, which provokes divine punishment. She dies and is buried at Kadesh (Numbers 20:1). The memory of her prophecy and leadership is kept alive in tradition: Micah 6:4 reminds that God sent her with Moses and Aaron to guide the people.
H4813G.portee: Mary shows that a woman can be a prophetess and spiritual leader in ancient Israel. Her example also teaches the limit of doubt towards those whom God establishes: her criticism of Moses, despite his status, brings divine judgment. For the Christian reader, she reminds that God chooses and confers authority, and that contesting it without reason incurs responsibility before Him.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:17
Sister of Shammai and Ishbah, daughter of Mered
H4813H.detail: Miriam is a woman belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. She is presented as the daughter of Mered and Bithiah, and as the sister of Shammai and Ishbah, which shows her connection to a family established in the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy.
H4813H.origine: The name Miriam means "rebellion" in Hebrew, derived from a root evoking opposition or protest. It is a name borne by several women in the Old Testament, the most famous being the elder sister of Moses and Aaron, a prophetess who led Israel in song after crossing the Red Sea.
H4813H.emploi: This Miriam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:17, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah dating from the period of the Divided Monarchy. She plays no narrative role but simply figures in the list of members of an established Judean family.

sens: Bitter and unpleasant taste of things
Grief, deep suffering that fills the soul
H4814.detail: 1. Bitterness is primarily a bitter and unpleasant taste, like that of certain plants or poison — a flavor that repulses. 2. Figuratively, bitterness describes moral suffering, the intense grief that fills the heart and mind. In Ezekiel 21:11, the prophet is commanded to groan "with bitterness in the soul" — this is not a simple sadness, but a deep affliction that permeates the whole being, like a detestable flavor that saturates the person's interior.
H4814.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be bitter" or "to cause pain." Bitterness is the state of one who has tasted something bitter — hence the very vivid image of misfortune that "fills the mouth" of the soul. The same root produces other words describing bitterness or divine wrath.
H4814.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 21:11, where it qualifies the manner in which the prophet must weep over the misfortunes of Israel. In this context, Ezekiel is ordered to groan not with a simple superficial regret, but with a visceral bitterness — a pain that invades the entire soul. This unique usage underscores the emotional and spiritual intensity of the prophetic groaning in the face of divine judgments.
H4814.portee: The bitterness of the soul, as expressed by Ezekiel, reminds the reader that authentic compassion in the face of sin and its consequences cannot be tepid or superficial. It engages the whole person, down to the deepest level. For the believer, this invites sincere repentance and truly painful intercession, not from hollow complaint, but from shared affliction that recognizes the gravity of evil.

sens: which is cruel, fierce, merciless
which causes an injury or intense suffering
which destroys or consumes with force
H4815.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses what is cruel and fierce, devoid of gentleness — it is the character of that which strikes mercilessly. In Deuteronomy 32:24, the "violent diseases" evoke plagues that strike the people like blows without mercy, alongside hunger and fever.
2. The second sense emphasizes the destructive intensity: a violent action deeply wounds, it consumes and destroys. The diseases in the text are not simply unpleasant; they ravage the body with brutal force.
3. Figuratively, what is violent sweeps everything in its path — it is the image of a force that meets no resistance and destroys.
H4815.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "bitterness" or "sourness." Bitterness is not just a taste: it evokes everything that is harsh, acrid, unbearable. Hence comes the idea of the violent — that which wounds like a bitter taste wounds the mouth, that which ravages like bitterness ravages the soul. It is an image that moves from the sensory (the bitter) to the moral and destructive.
H4815.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:24. It is part of the Song of Moses, where God enumerates the plagues that strike unfaithful Israel: hunger, fever, violent diseases, and attacks from wild beasts. The context shows that this qualifier designates not just a simple illness, but a fierce divine judgment, a punishment that falls mercilessly on the rebellious people.
H4815.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's justice is neither weak nor distracted: it operates with formidable force against infidelity and sin. For the believer, this sheds light on the gravity of the broken covenant and invites serious consideration of the divine word. It is a call not to despise God's warning.

sens: timidity, lack of courage
the state of one whose will is broken
moral or warrior cowardice
H4816.detail:
1. This word primarily denotes a weakness of heart, not physical but moral: it is the lack of courage, timidity in the face of danger. In Leviticus 26:36, God says He will make the hearts of the survivors "timid," meaning He will deprive them of warrior courage, so that the mere sound of a leaf will put them to flight.
2. It is also the state of a person whose will is broken, who has lost the moral strength to resist or act. This weakness does not come from a lack of physical strength, but from an inner failure, a dejection of the heart.
3. In the biblical context, it particularly expresses itself as cowardice in battle or before the enemy: it is the opposite of the valor and boldness that God demands from His people.
H4816.origine: The Hebrew word מֹרֶךְ (morekh) comes from a root that expresses the idea of softness, slackness, or weakening. It describes what loses its firmness, what becomes soft. Applied to the heart or soul, it evokes a heart that softens, that loses its temper, like a metal that has been softened in the fire. This image of softening well translates the spiritual reality: it is the heart that loses its moral strength.
H4816.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 26:36. There, God announces a curse: if His people disobey Him, He will strike the hearts of the survivors with timidity, so that they will flee at the slightest sound. It is a divine judgment where God removes courage from His rebellious people, symbolizing His abandonment. The context is that of the blessings and curses in Leviticus: the weakness of heart is foretold as a direct consequence of unfaithfulness.
H4816.portee: This word reminds us that true courage is not a purely human strength, but depends on the relationship with God. Timidity becomes the visible sign of divine judgment: when God withdraws, the heart softens and loses its temper. For the believer, this invites one to seek not in oneself, but in God, the moral strength to stand firm in the face of trials and spiritual enemies.

sens: vehicle drawn by horses, used in war or for transportation
seat or place where one sits in a vehicle or litter
H4817.detail:
1. The chariot is a wheeled vehicle, drawn by horses, very common in the Old Testament for war, transport, or royal display. Solomon had forty thousand chariots for his armies (1 Kings 4:26), which testifies to his military and economic power. It was a sign of wealth and prestige.
2. The word also refers to the seat or sitting place in such a vehicle, or the seat of a litter. The verse from the Song of Solomon (3:10) speaks of the "purple seat" of King Solomon, adorned with silver columns and a gold backrest: it is not about the chariot itself, but about the richly crafted throne or seat on which the king rests.
H4817.origine: The Hebrew word מֶרְכָּב (merkav) comes from the root רכב (rakav), which means "to ride, to mount." This is why מֶרְכָּב refers both to the vehicle one rides and the seat one sits on. The same root gives other words in the family: רָכִיב (rekiv, rider) and רָכַב (rakav, to ride a horse).
H4817.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in connection with royal or military prestige. In 1 Kings 4:26, it refers to Solomon's war chariots, a sign of his power. In Song of Solomon 3:10, it designates the royal seat adorned with precious stones and fine fabrics. In Leviticus 15:9, the context of ritual purity shows that the chariot was also an everyday object. The meaning thus varies between the vehicle itself and the ornamental seat that adorns it.
H4817.portee: This word reminds the believer that wealth and military power marked the reigns of the kings of Israel, particularly Solomon. It also invites reflection on what is glorious in the eyes of God: not the accumulation of chariots and horses, but justice and wisdom. See regarding this the reservations that the Law expresses about the desire for horses and chariots in a king.

sens: Wheeled vehicle drawn by horses, used in war or as a sign of power
Means of rapid transport or escape
Symbolic image of divine power or God's judgment
H4818.detail: 1. The chariot is a military and prestigious vehicle in biblical antiquity: drawn by horses, it was primarily used for war (Judges 4:15 where Sisera dismounted from his chariot to flee), but also to manifest royal authority (Genesis 41:43, where Pharaoh had Joseph ride in the chariot that followed his own to show his new dignity). 2. It is also a means of rapid movement for one fleeing danger or traveling in urgency: thus King Rehoboam mounted his chariot to escape from Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:18). 3. The Bible uses the chariot as a major image of divine power and dominion: God comes in fire, with chariots like a whirlwind (Isaiah 66:15), signifying that the Lord moves with irresistible force to execute His judgment.
H4818.origine: The Hebrew word merkavah comes from the root rakav which means "to ride, to mount" (this verb is found in Exodus 14:25 where the Egyptians ride in their chariots). Merkavah literally means "that on which one rides." The richness of the biblical vocabulary around the chariot (harness, horses, warriors) shows the strategic and symbolic importance of this vehicle in the life of the ancient Near East.
H4818.emploi: The word appears 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah). It primarily denotes the war chariot: the Egyptians launch their chariots against Israel at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:25, 15:4), and the kings of Israel maintain chariot garrisons (1 Kings 10:29). The chariot also marks status: riding in the chariot of the king or Pharaoh is an honor (Genesis 41:43, 2 Kings 10:15). Finally, the Bible transposes the chariot into prophetic language: it is the vehicle of the theophany, that is, of the manifestation of God (Isaiah 66:15, Zechariah 6:1-3 where Zechariah sees chariots coming out from between two mountains of bronze).
H4818.portee: The chariot reminds us that human power, even military and prestigious, is nothing compared to God's dominion. When the Bible speaks of the Lord's chariots coming to judge, it shows that true power does not belong to the kings of the earth, but to Him who reigns over all things. For the Christian, this invites one not to place trust in earthly forces, but to turn to God alone.

sens: Place where goods are bought and sold
Public space intended for commerce and exchanges
H4819.detail:
1. The market is the concrete place where commerce takes place: goods are brought there to be sold, and people come to buy. In Ezekiel 27:24, the prophet lists all the rich fabrics, blue embroidered cloaks, and cedar chests that merchants brought to the markets of Tyre, the great port city — all products intended for sale and exchange.
2. By extension, the market also refers to the commercial life itself, the activity of exchange in this public place. It is the space where the trade of a prosperous city pulses.
H4819.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְכֹּלֶת (markolet) derives from the root רכל, which evokes the idea of walking around, circulating, particularly for the purpose of commerce. The word thus refers to a place of commercial circulation, a spot where one goes back and forth to trade. This root expresses the movement of the merchant who moves to buy and sell.
H4819.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:24, in the famous context where the prophet depicts the wealth and extent of Tyre's commerce. Tyre was a renowned trading center, and its markets (in the plural in the text) attracted merchants from all over the world who brought their finest products: precious fabrics, dyed cloaks, embroideries. The term emphasizes the frenetic activity and commercial prominence of this powerful city.
H4819.portee: For the Christian reading Ezekiel, the word market reminds us that all wealth and prosperity, even those of the greatest cities, are fleeting. Tyre, so powerful in its commerce and luxury, will be judged and destroyed. This invites one not to place their heart in earthly riches, but in what lasts: the relationship with God.

sens: Intentional lie and dishonest action to deceive someone
Use of cunning or deception in trade, measurement, or weight
Unfair manner of acting, falsehood of words or deeds
Deception as a motive or inspiration for an act
H4820.detail:
1. Deception is primarily a deliberate act of lying: one deceives someone through false words or actions to mislead them. Jacob took Esau's blessing "by deceit" (Genesis 27:35) by pretending to be his brother. This is the heart of the word: the will to make someone believe the false.
2. The Bible often highlights deception in trade and measurement: a "false balance" is a rigged scale that gives a false weight (Proverbs 11:1, 20:23). It is the same dishonesty applied to exchanges and business.
3. Deception also describes a general attitude of moral falsehood: one who walks in deception does not speak with integrity. David begs God to listen to his "prayer made with lips free of deceit" (Psalms 17:1), meaning sincere and true. It is about being upright or deceiving.
4. In a more internal sense, deception is an inspiration, a motive that drives one to evil. Job swears that he has not "walked in deception" (Job 31:5), meaning he has not allowed this wicked intention to guide him.
H4820.origine: The Hebrew word מִרְמָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of throwing or projecting something — the image of a slope that deviates. Deception is what "deviates" the truth. This family of words is found in other contexts related to diversion or falsehood. The word appears mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets, where it denotes one of the great threats against just order and covenant.
H4820.emploi: The word מִרְמָה occurs 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms (12 times), Proverbs (9 times), and the prophets. It appears in three main contexts. First, as a personal or familial act: Jacob deceives his father (Genesis 27:35), Simeon and Levi deceive the people of Shechem (Genesis 34:13). Next, as commercial dishonesty: false balances, deceptive weights, unjust prices. Finally, and most frequently, as a characteristic of the words and conduct of the wicked, against whom the righteous asks God for a pure and upright heart. Daniel 11:23 also shows deception as a political tactic: a king will use deception and advance with few people.
H4820.portee: The Bible views deception as a serious violation of justice and covenant. It undermines the trust that binds the people to God and men to one another. For the Christian reader, this word calls for total honesty — in speech, in business, in every relationship — as a sign of the uprightness of one who walks with God. It is a call to sincerity of heart.

sens: A Benjamite from the time of the divided monarchy, son of Shaharaim and Hodesh
H4821.detail: Mirma is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reign of the divided monarchy (after the separation between the Northern and Southern kingdoms). He is the son of Shaharaim and Hodesh, and is part of a large sibling group: he has brothers Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuts, Sachia, Abitub, and Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:10). These brothers are listed as "heads of families," indicating that they held a position of responsibility within their respective clans.
H4821.origine: The name Mirma means "fraud" or "deception" in Hebrew. Although the meaning of the name evokes something negative, no particular information can be deduced about the character or actions of this individual. It is simply the name given to him at birth.
H4821.emploi: Mirma is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:10. He appears in a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, which lists the descendants of Shaharaim. According to the text, Mirma was born in the land of Moab, likely during a time when some Benjamites had left the land of Israel. The genealogical context suggests that he was a person of some importance since he is designated as a head of family.

sens: Priest and head of a family during the time of exile and return to Jerusalem
H4822G.detail: Merémoth is a proper name referring to a priest of Israel who played an important role during the return from exile to Babylon, in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah (around the 5th century BC). He appears in two closely related forms in the texts: Merémoth and Meraioth, which reflect slightly different pronunciations of the same name. The biblical uses present him performing several functions: first as a priest in charge of weighing the silver, gold, and sacred utensils brought back from Babylon (Ezra 8:33), then as a key figure in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:4 and 3:21), and finally among the heads of priestly families who seal the covenant of faithfulness to the Law (Nehemiah 10:5 and 12:3).
H4822G.origine: The name Merémoth literally means "elevations" in Hebrew, an image evoking height, exaltation, or high places. This meaning reflects the nobility of the priestly office: priests are called to a spiritual elevation in the service of the Temple. The name belongs to a family of Hebrew terms related to height and greatness.
H4822G.emploi: Merémoth appears five times in the texts of Ezra and Nehemiah, always as a figure of trust. In Ezra 8:33, he receives from Ezra himself the silver and the Temple objects — a responsibility that shows the high esteem in which he was held. In the two passages of Nehemiah 3, he is among the leaders working on the repair of the wall of Jerusalem, a sign of his involvement in the civil and religious reconstruction of the city. He is then mentioned among the signers of the covenant (Nehemiah 10 and 12), confirming his role as a leader in the returning community. These uses paint the portrait of a pious and reliable man, holding a prominent position.
H4822G.portee: Merémoth embodies faithfulness in restoration. At the time of the return from exile, when the people rebuild the Temple and the wall of Jerusalem, this man represents those who, despite the ruins and obstacles, dedicate themselves to restoring their faith and community. His example speaks to anyone who has had to rebuild their spiritual life after a period of distance.

sens: Priest son of Uriah, of the family of Koz, who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem
Temple servant during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah
H4822H.detail:
1. Merémoth is an active priest during the time of exile and the return to Jerusalem. He is the son of Uriah and belongs to the priestly family of Koz. His name literally means "elevations," likely evoking high places or elevated gifts.
2. In the accounts of Ezra and Nehemiah, Merémoth plays an important role in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is also mentioned for his service in the temple, assigned to the seventh division of priests.
H4822H.origine: The name Merémoth means "elevations" in Hebrew, formed from the root that designates what rises or is high. This name was borne by several characters during the return from exile to Jerusalem: at least three priests or Levites bore this name in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, reflecting the importance of this name in the priestly families of the return.
H4822H.emploi: Merémoth is mentioned in the lists of exiles who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. He appears in Ezra as a priest engaged in restoring the religious and civil life of Jerusalem. The text of Ezra 10:36 lists him among the notable priests of Ezra's time, thus contributing to the identity of the religious leaders of the return.
H4822H.portee: Merémoth represents those faithful men who, upon returning from exile, dedicated their energy to rebuilding both the walls and the spiritual life of Israel. His example shows the commitment of the people to restore worship and community after destruction and deportation.

sens: To walk on something, to trample it
To crush, to reduce to nothing by violence
To treat with contempt, to profane
H4823.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the action of walking on something, of trampling it: in Isaiah 7:25, the sheep trample the ground of an abandoned mountain; in Ezekiel 34:19, the sheep graze what other feet have trampled, that is, trampled upon.
2. The word also describes brutal crushing, destruction by trampling: in Isaiah 10:6, the invader tramples the people 'like the mud of the streets' — an image of reduction to nothing; in Isaiah 28:18, the covenant with death will not stand, and one will be 'trampled underfoot'.
3. By extension, to tread underfoot means to treat with contempt or to profane: in Daniel 8:13, the sanctuary is trampled — not only physically trampled but also profaned, desecrated.
H4823.origine: The word comes from a root meaning 'to walk' or 'to trample'. It first denotes the simple act of placing one's foot on the ground, then this repeated or violent action that crushes and destroys. The family of the word in Hebrew is rooted in the bodily image of the foot in action — a foot that walks, that treads, that crushes.
H4823.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mostly in Isaiah (4 times), where it describes the effects of divine anger and judgment. In Isaiah 5:5, God destroys His vineyard so that it may be trampled; in Isaiah 10:6, judgment takes shape in the enemy army that tramples the people. In Ezekiel 34:19, it is an abuse of shepherds: the weak must graze what the powerful have trampled. In Daniel 8:13, the sanctuary is profaned. The concrete sense (trampling) and the figurative sense (abusing, profaning) intertwine.
H4823.portee: This word reminds us that violent contempt and profanation have serious consequences before God. To tread underfoot is both to humiliate and to reduce to nothing; the Bible uses it to describe how sin crushes the weak and how divine judgment crushes the wicked. It is a stark image of the cost of injustice.

sens: Inhabitant of a place called Meronoth
Person originating from the region of Meronoth
H4824.detail: The word designates a man from a locality named Meronoth, probably located in Judea or nearby. In 1 Chronicles 27:30, Jechdia is referred to as 'Meronoth' (or 'Meronothite'), and he was in charge of King David's donkeys. In Nehemiah 3:7, Jadon the 'Meronothite' is listed among those who participated in the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. The term functions as a demonym, indicating the geographical or clan origin of a person, similar to how one would say 'Gibeonite' for an inhabitant of Gibeon.
H4824.origine: The name Meronoth designates a place whose probable Hebrew name was Merônôth or Merôn. The proper name 'Meronothite' is derived from this place, adding a suffix that means 'one who comes from'. This gentilice form (inhabitant of) is a common construction in biblical Hebrew to identify a person's origin.
H4824.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament. In both cases, it characterizes the origin or affiliation of a character. Jechdia, 'of Meronoth', was an officer of King David and managed the royal donkeys (1 Chronicles 27:30). Jadon the 'Meronothite' was one of the rebuilders of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:7). These two men seem to come from the same region, likely a town or district of Judea. However, the term remains rare, and the exact location of Meronoth remains uncertain for historians.

sens: One of the seven counselors of King Ahasuerus, who saw his face and held the highest rank in the kingdom.
H4825.detail: 1. Meres is one of the seven Persian and Median princes who formed the court and the inner council of King Ahasuerus during the exile of the Jews in Babylon. These seven counselors had the honor of seeing the king face to face and occupying the highest places in his kingdom, a mark of the highest political privilege (Esther 1:14).
H4825.origine: The name Meres means 'elevated' or 'lofty' in Hebrew, evoking the image of one who is of high dignity. It appears only once in the Bible, among the names of the seven royal counselors listed in the first chapter of Esther.
H4825.emploi: Meres is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 1:14, where he is named among the seven Persian princes who formed the council of King Ahasuerus. This enumeration of names serves to show the importance of the royal dignitaries and the political context of the Persian court at the time Esther becomes queen. These counselors represented the established power before Haman managed to gain his position of influence.
H4825.portee: This name reminds us that even the highest dignitaries of the world, those who saw the king and held the highest rank, are forgotten by history; only the name of Meres remains in Scripture, without any further details about his life. This invites the reader to reflect on the vanity of earthly honors and on the lasting power of the Word of God, which endures forever.

sens: One of the seven counselors of King Ahasuerus
H4826.detail: Marsena is one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who formed the council of King Ahasuerus. These men had the rare privilege of 'seeing the face of the king' — that is, having direct access to him — and held the highest rank in the kingdom (Esther 1:14). He represents the administrative and political elite of the Persian empire during the exile of the Jews.
H4826.origine: The name Marsena means 'worthy' or 'esteemed' in Persian. Its unique appearance in the Bible (Esther 1:14) indicates that he is a historical figure from the Persian context of the Babylonian captivity.
H4826.emploi: Marsena appears only once in the Bible, mentioned in Esther 1:14 among the seven counselors of King Ahasuerus. These counselors constitute the immediate circle of influence of the king and have authority over the affairs of the kingdom. Their presence alongside Ahasuerus underscores the political importance of the Persian royal court in the context of the book of Esther.

sens: Action or intention harmful, damaging
Deception, falsehood in words or thoughts
Misfortune, calamity
H4827.detail:
1. The word first denotes an action or intention aimed at harming, causing injury. It is the deliberate, thoughtful evil: in Daniel 11:27, the two kings 'seek in their hearts to do evil', meaning they conspire together to deceive one another and gain an advantage.
2. It can also mean deception or falsehood in words: those who do evil often do so by speaking falsely, hiding their true intentions. In the same verse, these kings 'will speak falsely' at the same table, which shows that the evil here includes duplicity.
3. The word can finally evoke the misfortune or calamity that results, the harm suffered.
H4827.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means 'to be bad' or 'to do harm'. It is related to the notion of damage or destruction. The form used in Daniel suggests a deliberate intention to harm, often accompanied by cunning or betrayal.
H4827.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 11:27. It describes the behavior of the two kings in conflict: although they speak to each other at the same table, each seeks to deceive the other and to carry out their plans at the expense of others. The context shows that this political evil—this strategic duplicity—will ultimately fail, for God controls history.
H4827.portee: This passage reminds the reader that betrayal, cunning, and malevolent intentions are never hidden from God and do not prosper eternally. Even when evil seems to succeed on earth, it is a lesson of trust: God maintains His plan despite the plots of men.

sens: One who shares life with another person, their equal in a relationship of friendship or closeness
One who accompanies someone in a particular circumstance or event
An intimate friend, in whom one has trust
The associate of a woman in the role of husband or brother-in-law
H4828.detail:
1. A companion is primarily someone who shares daily life with another person. In Genesis 26:26, Abimelech comes with Ahuzath, his "friend," which designates a close person in whom one has trust and with whom one maintains a personal relationship. It is a bond based on mutual esteem.
2. The word can also refer to one who stands by someone during an event. When Samson is invited to a wedding, he is given thirty "companions" (Judges 14:11) — men who accompany him and share the moment with him, without necessarily being his intimates.
3. A companion can be a trusted friend, someone reliable. In 2 Samuel 3:8, Abner recalls that he showed "kindness to the house of Saul, his brothers, and his 'friends,'" which evokes people from his circle of trust.
4. The term also applies to a husband or one who takes the place of a husband: when Samson's father gives his wife to a "companion" of Samson (Judges 14:20 and 15:2), the word designates one who takes his place as a spouse.
H4828.origine: The Hebrew word רֵעַ comes from a root that evokes the idea of being a friend, of regularly associating with someone. The family of the word includes terms that denote friendship and mutual association. It is a simple and common word in Hebrew, painting the image of a person with whom one maintains stable and trusting relationships.
H4828.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical narratives of the Old Testament. The Segond translates it sometimes as "companion" (when it refers to accompaniment or social role) and sometimes as "friend" (when trust or intimacy is emphasized). The uses in the book of Judges mainly show the companion as one who shares a moment (wedding, social event), while in 2 Samuel and Genesis, the bond leans more towards trust and friendship. The context of Judges 14-15 shows that this social bond could also have a legal dimension — the companion could take on responsibilities, such as taking the wife of a third party.
H4828.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of loyal and stable relationships in biblical life. A companion is not just an acquaintance: it is someone in whom one can place trust, who shares the journey with us. For the Christian reader, this evokes the model of sincere friendship, based on kindness and mutual faithfulness.

sens: grass and plants that livestock eat
grassland where animals graze
the action of grazing, feeding in a field
figuratively: spiritual nourishment
H4829.detail:
1. Pasture is primarily the grass and greenery that serve as food for sheep, goats, and herds. When Jacob asks Pharaoh for permission to settle in Egypt, he explains: "there is no pasture for your servants' sheep, for the famine weighs heavily on the land of Canaan" (Genesis 47:4). Without pasture, animals cannot survive.
2. It is also the land itself, the area where animals graze. The context clearly shows that the men of Judah "sought pastures for their flocks" and "found rich and good pastures" in a vast and peaceful land (1 Chronicles 4:39-40). It is a physical, defined place that can be conquered or lost.
3. Sometimes the word designates the very action of grazing. Job speaks of an animal that "roams the mountains to find its pasture" (Job 39:11): it refers to the food it eats while feeding.
4. Figuratively, the Bible uses this word to evoke spiritual nourishment or the good that one receives. God promises His people: "I will lead them to good pasture" (Ezekiel 34:14), an image of the protection and abundance He offers.
H4829.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to graze, to browse." The verb מרע (mara') expresses the action of eating grass. The word מִרְעֶה retains this fundamental idea: the place where animals do what they do naturally, feed on plants. This root is found in occupational names: a shepherd is one who makes animals graze. The image is very concrete, rooted in the pastoral life of the ancient Near East.
H4829.emploi: This word appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narrative and poetic passages. It is found when families seek good lands for their flocks (Genesis, 1 Chronicles), in descriptions of wealth and prosperity, and in poems that lament drought or famine. Job uses it to speak of wild animals; Isaiah and Ezekiel use it figuratively to describe the good that God gives to His people or that is expected from Him. The word always retains its pastoral, concrete color, never abstract.
H4829.portee: For the biblical people of shepherds and herders, pasture is not a detail: it is life itself. Understanding this word reminds us that survival depended on land and nature. When the Bible speaks of "good pasture" or God leading us to pasture, it uses a very simple and strong image: having what is needed to live in abundance and peace. It is an invitation to see God as the one who provides, who gives all that we need.

sens: Grassland where animals graze
The action of grazing a flock
The whole flock that grazes
H4830.detail:
1. Pasture is primarily a concrete place: a meadow, a grassy area where sheep and goats find food. It is the simplest biblical image: in Israel, shepherds led their animals to the hills and fields to graze (Isaiah 49:9: "they will find pastures on all the hills").
2. The word also designates the action of grazing, that is, the care and management of the flock by the shepherd. It is a responsibility, a pastoral task that must nourish and protect the animals.
3. By extension, pasture can refer to the flock itself, the whole group of animals that are grazed. Thus the "flocks" in Jeremiah 10:21 are the animals that scatter when the shepherds are foolish and negligent.
H4830.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root רעה (ra'a), which means "to graze" or "to make graze." This root evokes the fundamental action of the shepherd. It is related to other biblical words for shepherd (רֹעֶה, ro'é) and pastures (מִרְעִית, mir'it). In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates situations of pastoral care and nourishment of God's people.
H4830.emploi: This word appears about 10 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and the prophets. The Psalms use it spiritually: the people of Israel are described as the "flock" of God's pasture, meaning that God Himself is the shepherd who nourishes and leads His people (Psalms 74:1, 79:13, 95:7, 100:3). The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah use it in a context of pastoral responsibility: true pastures nourish (Isaiah 49:9), while bad shepherds allow the flocks to scatter (Jeremiah 10:21, 23:1). The meaning varies between the concrete place and the spiritual metaphor of the people entrusted to God.
H4830.portee: For the believer, this word reveals a deep truth: God is not a distant master, but an attentive shepherd who nourishes and leads His people as a shepherd cares for his flock. This humble and concrete image reassures: it shows that God provides for our needs and protects us. It also denounces bad religious leaders who, like the foolish shepherds of Jeremiah, neglect the people entrusted to their care.

sens: Geographical landmark or reference point on the border of the territory of Zebulun
H4831.detail: Mareala is a site or reference point located on the boundary of the territory assigned to the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the Promised Land. In the passage that mentions it (Joshua 19:11), it serves as a reference point to describe the route of the border: "The boundary of their inheritance extended to Sarid. It went westward to Mareala, and touched Dabbesheth." Its name evokes the idea of trembling or instability, which could refer to a place characterized by earthquakes or a shifting geography (cliffs, landslides), although the biblical text does not specify anything further about its exact nature.
H4831.origine: The name Mareala comes from a Hebrew root meaning to tremble or oscillate (the idea of trembling is found in other words of the same family). Its meaning suggests a site or natural landmark that is unstable or remarkable geologically, which would have served as a visible and distinctive reference point for territorial boundaries.
H4831.emploi: Mareala appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:11, during the description of the territory assigned to Zebulun. It is included in a list of landmarks that delineate the borders of this tribe. Like many geographical markers in the Old Testament, it situates and defines Israel's territorial inheritance in the Promised Land. Today, the exact site of Mareala remains difficult to identify with certainty on the archaeological map of the region.

sens: Restoration of the body after illness or injury
Remedy, that which heals and restores health
State of physical and mental well-being
Calmness, tranquility of heart and mind
H4832.detail:
1. **Restoration of the body**: The word primarily refers to the act of healing, regaining lost health. It is the process by which an illness or wound ceases. In 2 Chronicles 21:18, King Jehoshaphat suffers from a "no remedy" illness, meaning there is no means of healing.
2. **Remedy, that which heals**: The word can also denote that which heals, the means or substance that restores. Proverbs 12:18 states that "the tongue of the wise brings healing" — here, it is the wise word itself that acts as a remedy against the wounds caused by harmful words.
3. **Well-being of body and soul**: The term extends to the general state of health and balance. Proverbs 4:22 asserts that wisdom "is health to all their flesh": it provides not only life but also physical and moral integrity.
4. **Calmness and inner peace**: The word also describes the calming of the heart and mind. Proverbs 14:30 says, "A calm heart is life to the body" — this inner peace acts as a healing that revitalizes the whole being.
H4832.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to heal" or "to repair." It is from the same family as the word "rph" (rafah), which expresses the idea of restoring what is broken or deteriorated. In the Greek Old Testament, this term often translates the biblical concept of total restoration — physical and spiritual — the restoration of the harmony that God desires for His creatures.
H4832.emploi: This word appears about 15 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the wisdom books (Proverbs) and in the prophets. In Proverbs, it regularly returns to show how wisdom, gentle words, and a peaceful heart produce healing and health — which includes both body and soul. In Jeremiah (8:15, 14:19, 33:6), the prophet uses it to speak of the healing of Israel, the physical and spiritual restoration expected from God. In Malachi 4:2, the Sun of righteousness brings healing in its wings. The word thus denotes both concrete medical cure and the spiritual restoration of the people.
H4832.portee: This word teaches the believer that healing comes from God — whether physical, through divine wisdom, or the restoration of the people. It also shows how wise words and a peaceful heart are concrete means by which God works for our good. For the reader, it is an invitation to seek from God, in His wisdom and in the peace He offers, the true restoration of the whole being.

sens: That which pollutes, that which makes water or a liquid dirty
State of that which has become muddy, mixed with mud or impurities
Figuratively: that which causes moral or spiritual pollution
H4833.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes mud or deposits that disturb the water and make it murky. In Ezekiel 34:19, the sheep must drink "what your feet have troubled": the negligent shepherds have walked in the water, leaving mud and dirt, making undrinkable what should have been pure.
2. It is the state of that which has been made muddy or soiled by passage, by walking. The image is that of a flock finding to eat and drink what the bad shepherds have already contaminated by their carelessness.
3. Spiritually, this symbolizes moral corruption: pastors who, instead of nourishing and protecting their people, pollute them by their bad example or negligence.
H4833.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of treading, walking on something with the feet. The trouble of the liquid thus arises from the passage of feet that stir up the mud and sediments. This same root evokes the action of walking, treading, hence the image of pollution by trampling.
H4833.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 34:19. In this passage, the prophet reproaches the shepherds of Israel for their negligence: instead of properly feeding and preserving the purity of all that the flock depends on (food and water), they have contaminated it. This unique usage is part of a long accusation against the bad shepherds who exploit or abandon the people. The word embodies the image of waste, of culpable negligence that renders unworthy what should be good.
H4833.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that the responsibility of spiritual leaders is serious: they must not only enrich themselves or neglect their duties, but protect and preserve the moral and spiritual purity of the people. The condemnation of the polluted shepherds invites everyone to examine whether they contribute to building up or corrupting those around them.

sens: Who strikes hard, with force and intensity
Who injures, causing physical or moral pain
Who is serious, grave and distressing
Who is sharp, cutting in tone or speech
H4834.detail: 1. The primary meaning of the word is that of something that strikes or hits with force: the "violent" curses pronounced against David (1 Kings 2:8) are harsh and cutting words intended to wound. 2. It also describes a physical or moral pain that imposes itself with intensity: in Micah 2:10, the "violent pains" evoke a suffering that weighs heavily on the one who experiences it. 3. The word can qualify what is true or serious in the sense of "delivering a decisive blow": Job asks his friends if their "true" words (Job 6:25) are persuasive—these are words that strike true, that have weight. 4. An "irritation" (Job 16:3) is a response that stings, that annoys, as if it hits head-on the one who hears it.
H4834.origine: The Hebrew verb מָרַץ (maratz) comes from a root evoking the idea of striking, injuring, or causing pain. It is close to the idea of something that imposes itself with force and leaves a mark. The word describes less a massive physical violence than a quality of what penetrates, wounds, or weighs down: a sharp word, a persistent pain, an illness that weakens. This is why translations vary according to context (violent, true, irritation), but all refer to this idea of an intensity that imposes itself.
H4834.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Old Testament, always in contexts of suffering, harsh words, or discomfort. In 1 Kings 2:8, it qualifies the curses that Shimei hurled against David—words filled with hatred and hostility. In Job 6:25 and 16:3, it describes the penetrating quality of words: the "true" persuasive words that strike true, and the "irritation" of empty responses that annoy. In Micah 2:10, it applies to the "violent pains" that accompany devastation. The word thus combines the idea of force, pain, and moral impact: what strikes, what wounds, what weighs down.
H4834.portee: This word reminds us that words have power: they can wound like a weapon (the curses of Shimei), they can convince when they are true (the words of Job), or they can irritate and be vain when they come from a lack of understanding. It invites us to measure the weight and quality of our own words, and to recognize the suffering that can be caused by pains—whether physical or moral—when they impose themselves with an inevitable intensity.

sens: Action of mistreating someone by force
Brutal injustice committed against the weak
H4835.detail:
1. The word designates the action of submitting someone by force and brutality, breaking or crushing them morally and physically. In Jeremiah 22:17, the king of Judah is condemned because he "exercises violence": he uses his power to oppress, mercilessly mistreating those under his authority.
2. More broadly, it is cruel and deliberate injustice, the abuse of force against the weak to profit from them or satisfy one's desires. The prophet presents this violence alongside greed and murder: these are the sins of the tyrant who seeks only his personal gain, with no respect for life or the rights of others.
H4835.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes crushing, destruction. It belongs to the family of words that describe breaking or fracturing—the idea of a force that shatters and reduces to nothing. It is a strong term, depicting oppression not merely as an injustice, but as a physical and moral aggression.
H4835.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament: in Jeremiah 22:17. It is found in a passage where the prophet denounces King Jehoiakim for having "his eye and heart set on injustice," meaning he is wholly preoccupied with his personal enrichment. The violence he exercises is presented as the fruit of this corruption of heart, as the visible manifestation of greed and impiety. It is a term that prophets use to qualify the crimes of oppressors.
H4835.portee: This word reminds the reader that violence and oppression, although they may seem to triumph in the eyes of the world, are seen by God as an abomination—especially when they come from those who have the power to protect. Jeremiah's denunciation of the king shows that God does not tolerate the abuse of power, and holds especially accountable those who mistreat the weak.

sens: Sharp metal instrument used for piercing
Tool used to mark or pierce a surface
Figuratively: that which marks deeply
H4836.detail:
1. A punch is a sharp, solid metal instrument that is driven into a material to pierce or penetrate it. It is the tool of the carpenter or blacksmith. In Exodus and Deuteronomy, the punch is used to pierce the ear: it is a very concrete, painful gesture that leaves a permanent mark (Exodus 21:6).
