H4872.emploi: Moses appears 704 times in the Bible, primarily in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. He is first a saved child raised in the court of Egypt (Exodus 2), then a man on the run who encounters God (Exodus 3). From Exodus 5 onward, he becomes the leader and mediator between God and Israel: he announces the plagues to Pharaoh, organizes the crossing of the Red Sea, receives the Law at Sinai, and manages the people's crises in the desert. In Deuteronomy 33:4, it is written: "Moses gave us the law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob," summarizing his role as lawgiver. The Gospels and the New Testament constantly cite him as a reference for the first covenant.
H4872.portee: Moses embodies faithfulness to God's call despite obstacles, courageous intercession for others, and faithful transmission of the received Word. His example shows that God can call anyone, even an imperfect man with doubts or weaknesses, to accomplish His purposes. For the Christian, Moses remains a key figure: Jesus Himself is compared to Moses as a prophet and mediator of a new covenant.

sens: The prophet and lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt
The man through whom God gave the Law at Sinai
The author of the books of the Law recognized by Jewish and Christian tradition
H4873.detail:
1. Moses is the great prophet and deliverer of the people of Israel. According to Exodus, he was born to a family of Levites, saved by Pharaoh's daughter, and became the leader who brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt. Brother of Aaron the priest and Miriam, married to Zipporah, father of Gershom and Eliezer, he embodies the deliverance that God works for His people.
2. Moses is the mediator between God and Israel: it is to him that God gave the Ten Commandments and all the Law on Mount Sinai. For forty years, he guided the people in the desert, receiving God's instructions and transmitting them.
3. His name, which means "drawn from the waters," recalls the story of his discovery as a baby in a basket floating on the Nile. Biblical and Jewish tradition attributes to Moses the authorship of the first five books of the Bible (the Law or Torah). In Ezra 6:18, he is still referred to as the author of the "book of Moses" to which one refers to know the divine prescriptions.
H4873.origine: The Hebrew name Moshèh (מֹשֶׁה) literally means "drawn" or "the one who is drawn": it evokes the image of the newborn taken out of the water of the Nile. This etymology is evident in the account of Exodus 2:10, where Pharaoh's daughter gives this name to the rescued child. It is a theophoric name that signals the action of divine rescue from his infancy.
H4873.emploi: Moses is the foundational figure of the Old Testament, mentioned for the first time in Exodus 2:10. He appears prominently in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, as well as throughout the history of Israel. In Ezra 6:18, he is cited as the author of the divine books to which one still refers after the Exile, showing that his legislative authority remains central for the restored community. Moses is the biblical type of prophet, liberator, and mediator of the Covenant: in this capacity, Jesus is sometimes presented as a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15).
H4873.portee: For the Christian, Moses embodies the salvific power of God who frees His people from servitude and gives them a Law to shape them in holiness. His story reveals that God prepares His servants and calls them to missions that exceed human strength. At the same time, the Law given by Moses shows the standard of divine justice: it prepares the way for grace and the coming of Christ, who will fulfill and transform what Moses inaugurated.

sens: One who has lent money to someone else
A person who has the right to demand repayment of a debt
H4874.detail:
1. The creditor is the person who has granted a loan of money or goods to another. This is the one who expects to be repaid. In Deuteronomy 15:2, every creditor who has lent to his neighbor must cancel his claim during the year of release.
2. It is also the person who legally holds the right to demand payment of his debt. However, this right is not absolute: the law of Moses commands the creditor to grant forgiveness every seven years, which shows that compassion takes precedence over financial interest.
H4874.origine: The Hebrew word mashé comes from the root that means "to let go" or "to release." It designates the one to whom a release is made, that is, the one whose debt is canceled. The context of the release (shemita) in the sabbatical year is central to understanding this word: it reveals that even the creditor, who has the right to demand, must learn forgiveness and generosity towards his poorer brother.
H4874.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 15:2, in the passage concerning the release of the seventh year. The law stipulates that every creditor must relinquish his rights over the debt of an Israelite during this sabbatical year. This unique usage underscores the critical importance of this commandment in the social life of Israel: it is an act of social justice and brotherhood, where even one who legally has the right to demand must accept loss to honor God's plan and help the brother in need.
H4874.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on the grace of forgiving debts, both in financial and spiritual terms. Jesus will take up this teaching when he teaches us to ask God to forgive our debts as we forgive our debtors. It is a call to mercy: the one who has the power to demand chooses instead to give, thus imitating the heart of God who has forgiven us our greatest debt.

sens: A barren and arid place, without water or vegetation
State of physical and material devastation
State of abandonment and solitude
Total destruction caused by divine judgment
H4875.detail: 1. The word designates a naturally arid and barren place, devoid of water and incapable of sustaining vegetation: it is the image of the "dry places" where God causes rain to fall (Job 38:27), these parched lands that can only be traversed in desperation. 2. It can also describe the devastation of a once habitable place, reduced by misery to a state of ruin: impoverished men "flee to the dry places, long abandoned and desolate" (Job 30:3), that is, devastated regions where living is a torment. 3. The idea expands to anything that is empty and desolate, invaded by absence: a heart drained of resources, a territory abandoned by its inhabitants. 4. Applied to divine judgment, the word expresses total destruction and annihilation: the day of the Lord will be a "day of ruin and destruction" (Zephaniah 1:15), that is, a catastrophe that leaves everything in ruins, barren and empty.
H4875.origine: The word comes from a root meaning literally "to be dry" or "to be empty." This root evokes the primary image of desiccation: a land that has lost all moisture becomes barren, inhospitable, abandoned. The word gradually enriches to designate not only the physical character of aridity but also the spiritual or moral state of devastation: what was fertile, populated, and alive becomes a dried-up nothingness.
H4875.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 30:3, it describes desert areas where the miserable take refuge. In Job 38:27, it designates the arid regions of creation that God provides with water and greenery. In Zephaniah 1:15, it characterizes the final judgment as a destruction ravaging everything, comparable to a desert: a universe emptied, barren, doomed to chaos. These usages progressively move from the concrete (a lifeless landscape) to the eschatological (final annihilation).
H4875.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God does not want our lives to become spiritual deserts. It is also a word of consolation: God "waters the solitary places" (Job 38:27), showing that He never abandons what seems barren. Finally, Zephaniah uses this word to warn that divine judgment will turn everything into ruins for those who ignore it — a powerful motivation for conversion.

sens: Complete destruction of a place, city, or building
State of dilapidation and abandonment that results
Fall and annihilation of a person or a people
H4876.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the total physical destruction of a place: a building, a city, or a sanctuary reduced to nothing by violence, war, or divine judgment. In Psalms 73:18, those who reject God are placed "on slippery paths" and brought to ruin: the image is that of a fall that destroys everything.
2. It also evokes the state of desolation that follows: abandoned, devastated places where only debris remains. Psalms 74:3 speaks of places "constantly devastated," that is, regularly ravaged and left in a state of ruin.
3. Figuratively, the word applies to the ruin of a person or a people: their moral fall, their spiritual or political annihilation. This is what threatens those who turn away from God.
H4876.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of ravaging, destroying. It is related to terms that mean "to devastate" or "to annihilate." Its basic image is that of collapse and emptiness: something that was built, organized, becomes a field of desolation.
H4876.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in the Psalms. In Psalms 73:18, it describes the fall of those who live without God: they slip and fall into ruin. In Psalms 74:3, it designates the sanctuary of Jerusalem constantly ravaged, likely by the enemies of Israel. In both cases, ruin is the result of divine judgment or enemy assault; it is irreparable and total.
H4876.portee: For the psalmist and for us, ruin reminds us that God's judgment on sin is real and complete. It also shows how holy places can be profaned and destroyed. The word invites us to take seriously the threat of judgment and to seek protection in God, rather than following slippery paths.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon
H4877.detail: Meshobab is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:34. He appears in a genealogy, alongside Jamlech and Josha son of Amatzia, among the descendants of Simeon.
H4877.origine: The name Meshobab literally means "restored" or "returned" (from the Hebrew verb shub, "to return"). This meaning evokes the idea of a return or restoration, although we know nothing of what this represented for this individual.
H4877.emploi: Meshobab appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:34, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Simeon. He plays no narrative role and is mentioned only to record the families of this tribe during the time of the divided monarchy.

sens: turning away, distancing oneself
abandonment of the covenant with God
apostasy, rebellion against God
stubbornness in evil
habitual disposition to deny God
H4878.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical movement of turning away, turning one's back, and leaving: it is to refuse to remain face to face. In Hosea 11:7, God says that His people "are inclined to turn away from me."
2. Applied to the relationship with God, it means breaking the covenant, the pact that God made with Israel: it is a breach of faithfulness towards the one who bound Himself to His people. In Jeremiah 3:6, the prophet calls Israel "the unfaithful one" because she has betrayed the commitment made at Sinai.
3. It is apostasy: a deliberate refusal to acknowledge God, an act of rebellion. Jeremiah 3:11 contrasts unfaithful Israel with treacherous Judah, showing two forms of betrayal.
4. The word also describes stubbornness: the person who becomes unfaithful does not change; they persist. In Jeremiah 8:5, it is written that this people "gives itself to perpetual wanderings."
5. Finally, it is an inclination, a tendency of the heart: the natural propensity of the sinner to turn away from God and His commandments (Jeremiah 3:22, where God calls to return from "unfaithfulness").
H4878.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to turn, to turn away." It evokes the gesture of someone who turns their back: one imagines someone who was facing God and who suddenly pivots and leaves. Infidelity is therefore not primarily a secret thought, but a visible action: it is the back turned. This root is also that of the verb "to repent" or "to return": infidelity and repentance are two opposing movements of the same body.
H4878.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophets Jeremiah and Hosea, who denounce the sin of Israel. In Jeremiah, this term repeatedly qualifies Israel herself ("the unfaithful one") and her repeated acts ("your unfaithfulness"). The context is always that of idolatry and abandonment of the worship of the true God: Israel prostitutes herself on the mountains (Jeremiah 3:6), she turns away despite the calls of the prophets (Jeremiah 8:5). Hosea also uses the word to show how God calls His people to return, as one recalls a child who escapes (Hosea 11:7). It is a reproach at the heart of classical prophecy: you had promised, you are distancing yourself.
H4878.portee: This word reminds the believer that faithfulness to God is not a matter of vague feeling, but of orientation: to remain face to face with God or to turn one's back on Him. Infidelity is apostasy, an act that has visible consequences. But the context of the prophets also shows that God always calls for return: even the unfaithful can "return" and find the way. It is a word of judgment, but also of hope for the one who repents.

sens: Fault, deviation from truth or what is right
Responsibility for having made a mistake
H4879.detail:
1. The word denotes a fault or a wandering, a deviation from truth or righteousness. It conveys the idea of having been mistaken, of having missed the goal. In Job 19:4, Job asserts that if he has truly sinned, he alone bears the error — he takes responsibility for his fault.
2. By extension, it can denote guilt or the responsibility for having committed this error. It is the one who has strayed who must answer for it.
H4879.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of straying, of being mistaken, of deviating from the right path. It belongs to a family of words that revolve around error and wandering. The basic notion is that of a deviation, a divergence from what is right and true.
H4879.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 19:4. Job, suffering and accused by his friends of sinning, defends his innocence by saying that if he truly had sinned, he alone would be responsible — the error would be his and he would bear its weight. It is a rare word that emphasizes the idea of personal guilt in the face of a fault committed.
H4879.portee: This passage reminds the believer that one cannot shift the responsibility for their errors onto others or onto God. Each person is accountable for their own faults. It is a call to honesty and humility in the face of our shortcomings, as Job himself shows by acknowledging that if the reproach were founded, he would fully assume it.

sens: long flat stick used to propel a boat or ship
the working instrument of the sailor or boatman
H4880A.detail:
1. The oar is this long, flat stick that is plunged into the water to propel and steer a boat. In Ezekiel 27:29, during the destruction of the merchant ship of Tyre, all the sailors who handled the oar descend from their ships: this indicates that the oar is the fundamental instrument of their trade, the sign that they are men of the sea.
2. By extension, the word designates the one who handles the oar, the boatman or sailor himself, taken in his role as a worker of the waters. He is a man of toil, dedicated to the service of the ship.
H4880A.origine: The Hebrew word מָשׁוֹט (mashôt) comes from a root that means to strike, to graze, or to push — the very gesture of moving the oar through the water. It is a concrete and vivid word, which depicts the action before the tool: it first speaks of the act of rowing.
H4880A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:29, in the poetic description of the fall of Tyre, a great commercial power. The text enumerates all the people of the port who descend from their ships during the disaster: sailors, pilots, and then those who handle the oar. It is a word of narrative imagery, belonging to the language of navigation and maritime commerce of the ancient East.
H4880A.portee: This verse reminds the reader that all human power, even that of a rich and dominant city, rests on men who work and depend on conditions they do not control. The oar is the humble tool of the worker, and it is through these workers that empires are built or fall apart.

sens: Flat stick fixed to the edge of a boat to propel and steer it in the water
Object of prestige for a merchant or warship
H4880B.detail:
1. The oar is a long flat piece of wood that is plunged into the water and operated to move a boat forward. It is the lever arm that transforms human force into the movement of the ship. In Ezekiel 27:6, the oars of the great merchant ship of Tyre are made of oak from Bashan, a wood renowned for its strength, which shows their importance for the maneuvering of the vessel.
2. The oar also becomes a symbol of wealth and naval power: it equips merchant ships and prestigious fleets. The care given to the construction of the oars of the ship of Tyre — with noble materials like Bashan oak — reveals that it was an element of luxury and maritime prestige.
H4880B.origine: The Hebrew word miššôt is related to the family of verbs meaning "to strike" or "to hit" — the oar, which strikes the water to propel the boat, carries in some way this sense of the repeated blow. It is a variant form of the word māšôt (H4880A), both translating the simple and ancient idea of an instrument that pushes the ship: the repetitive and rhythmic gesture of rowing, which dates back to the beginnings of navigation.
H4880B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:6, in the poetic and detailed description of the great commercial ship of Tyre at the height of its splendor. This passage enumerates the prestigious materials that composed this ship — rare woods, worked ivory, distant islands — and the oars made of Bashan oak are included in this gallery of maritime luxury. The context is that of a prophetic meditation on the wealth and fall of Tyre, the quintessential trading city.
H4880B.portee: For the reader, this humble mention of the oars in a ship description reminds us that every element of the ship — even the working instrument — could be a work of art and a sign of power. It concretely illustrates how Tyre had made navigation and commerce an expression of its genius and wealth before its judgment.

sens: Fence made of intertwined bushes or thorns
Natural barrier that obstructs or slows passage
Figurative obstacle on the path of life
H4881A.detail:
1. A hedge is a living fence formed by tightly packed bushes or thorns. It is a natural barrier found in fields or along paths. In Proverbs 15:19, the sluggard sees his path of life hindered by a hedge of thorns — an image indicating that his laziness creates unavoidable obstacles.
2. The word also evokes the idea of a barrier that blocks or makes passage difficult. While the sluggard faces a hedge of thorns, the path of the righteous is smooth: no obstacles, no friction.
3. Figuratively, the hedge represents everything that slows us down or discourages us in our spiritual efforts. It is a portrait of how our choices (like laziness) build the walls that imprison us.
H4881A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of cutting or dividing — which reminds us that the hedge is a feature of separation, a boundary. The thorn hedge is very present in the imagery of the ancient Near East, where it represents both protection of the field and a formidable obstacle.
H4881A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 15:19. It is used in contrast to the smooth path of the righteous: laziness erects hedges of thorns, while righteousness creates easy paths. The image is that of a life path made impassable by neglect and inactivity.
H4881A.portee: This image shows the reader how our habits and choices construct our reality. The sluggard does not encounter misfortune or persecution from God — it is his own actions that erect thorny obstacles. Conversely, righteousness smooths the path. It is a call to act with wisdom and effort to lead to a fluid and prosperous life.

sens: Fence made of bushes or thorny plants
Protection or boundary built around a property
H4881B.detail:
1. A hedge is a living barrier, composed of bushes or thorny plants, that surrounds a piece of land. In Isaiah 5:5, the prophet describes a vineyard protected by a hedge: God threatens to remove this hedge so that the vineyard may be grazed and trampled, meaning delivered to destruction.
2. Figuratively, the hedge represents divine protection or boundary. It symbolizes God's guard that separates His people from danger or marks the borders of His property.
H4881B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to close" or "to shut." The hedge is the natural image of a living fence, common in the East where vineyards are cultivated in enclosed and guarded lands. This type of protection was essential to preserve vineyards from wild animals and intruders.
H4881B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 5:5. It is part of the parable of the Lord's vineyard, where God describes the care He has given to His people (Israel): He planted it, surrounded it with a protective hedge, and kept it. The removal of the hedge symbolizes the withdrawal of divine protection due to the people's unfaithfulness.
H4881B.portee: This image of the hedge being removed reminds us that God's protection is not guaranteed eternally, but depends on the faithfulness of His people. It invites the reader to consider divine guard as a precious gift and not to take it for granted. The vineyard that loses its hedge becomes vulnerable: similarly, a people that strays from God deprives itself of His protection.

sens: Woodworking or cutting tool consisting of a toothed blade
Figuratively, instrument of power in the hands of God
H4883.detail:
1. A saw is a manual tool with a toothed blade, used for cutting wood or stone. In Isaiah 10:15, it represents a concrete instrument of human labor, alongside the axe or the staff.
2. In the prophetic passage of Isaiah, the saw becomes an image of the instrument that God uses to accomplish His purposes: it should not boast of its power, for it acts only in the hand of the one who wields it. It is a lesson in humility addressed to human powers that forget that God uses them according to His will.
H4883.origine: The Hebrew word massor comes from a root meaning "to saw" or "to cut." It is a name simply designating this well-known tool in ancient Israel, where wood was shaped for construction, furniture, and Temple sacrifices.
H4883.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 10:15. This prophetic passage is part of God's judgment against Assyria: the prophet compares instruments of war and domination to mere tools that owe their effectiveness only to the one who holds them. The saw thus symbolizes all human power devoid of divine wisdom.
H4883.portee: This verse teaches believers that true power does not reside in weapons or human instruments, but in God's will. It calls for humility: those who accomplish great things should never believe it is by their own strength, but recognize that God guides and uses them for His purposes.

sens: Determined quantity of liquid or material
Standard for weighing or evaluating
Fixed portion assigned
Limit or restraint exercised
H4884.detail:
1. The word first designates a precise quantity of liquid or solid substance, measured with a standard. In Ezekiel 4:11, the prophet must drink water "by the measure of a sixth of a hin" (the hin is a Hebrew unit): a determined portion, neither more nor less.
2. More broadly, it is the instrument or system by which a quantity is determined — a standard of weight, volume, or length. Leviticus 19:35 commands not to commit iniquity "in measures of dimension, weights, and measures of capacity": it concerns just tools or norms.
3. The word can also designate an assigned or fixed portion, like a ration of bread or water distributed. In Ezekiel 4:16, besieged Jerusalem must eat "bread by weight and with anxiety" and drink "water by measure and with dread": each inhabitant receives a rationed portion, a sign of famine.
4. Finally, "measure" can express restraint, an imposed limitation — the idea that something is regulated, framed, and not left to whim.
H4884.origine: The Hebrew word מְשׂוּרָה (mesurah) comes from the root משׁר (meshar) which means "to measure" or "to extend." It is related to the image of delimiting, fixing a precise extent or quantity. In Hebrew, the corresponding verb and words of the same family all express the idea of determining with accuracy: establishing a norm, a limit, a portion.
H4884.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the concrete sense of "measured quantity" or "standard." In Leviticus 19:35, it is part of a legal context of commercial and religious honesty: God commands that weights and measures be just, neither false nor deceptive. In 1 Chronicles 23:29, it describes the tasks of the Levites in the service of the Temple, notably the preparation of bread and cakes "in all measures of capacity and length": it is the technical and ritual aspect. In Ezekiel 4:11 and 4:16, the word takes on a dramatic hue: it is the rationed portion of water and bread imposed on the prophet to symbolize the siege and famine of Jerusalem. In each occurrence, the word designates a determined quantity, never vague or approximate.
H4884.portee: This word reminds the believer that God demands justice and honesty even in material details: weights, measures, and commercial exchanges are not places where one can cheat. It also evokes the reality of divine judgment — each will receive their portion, their just measure — and the importance of recognizing the limits that God imposes: sufficiency, not excess, discipline, not abandonment.

sens: Feeling of happiness and inner satisfaction
Pleasure that something or someone provides
Festivity or collective rejoicing
State of cheerfulness and joyfulness
Delight or enjoyment
H4885.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the feeling of happiness and satisfaction that fills the heart. It is a deep inner joy, like that which a bride feels for her groom (Isaiah 62:5), or that which a father would feel for his child.
2. It can also refer to the pleasure or enjoyment that a person or thing provides to someone else — what a person's "ways" provide to those who follow them, for example (Job 8:19).
3. The word is also used for collective rejoicing, the festivities of a city or an entire nation. When the Bible says that "joy has disappeared" or that "gladness is banished from the land," it speaks of feasts, songs, and public celebrations (Isaiah 24:11).
4. Sometimes the word more broadly denotes a state of cheerfulness, the absence of sadness and mourning — which is why Jerusalem and those who love her are invited to "rejoice with her" (Isaiah 66:10).
5. In a few rare cases, it simply refers to the idea of delight or enjoyment, the pleasure found in something — like the wild donkeys that will "play" in the abandoned ruins (Isaiah 32:14).
H4885.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of rejoicing, of finding pleasure. It belongs to the same family as other words expressing joy and happiness in the Old Testament. The initial image is that of the heart rising, flourishing — a feeling that manifests life, vigor, and blessing.
H4885.emploi: This word appears about 16 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel) and in the Psalms. The Bible uses it to speak of human joy — that of a loved one, that of a city — but also to evoke the absence of joy, its annihilation. When Jerusalem suffers, it is said that her joy disappears (Lamentations 2:15; Lamentations 5:15). Conversely, the prophet calls for future, restored joy: the people will "rejoice" again with Jerusalem (Isaiah 66:10). The word is also used to designate feasts, celebrations, and the well-being of an entire community.
H4885.portee: This word reminds the believer that joy is a fundamental biblical good — not a superficial lightness, but a state of the heart rooted in satisfaction and peace. The Bible does not see joy as a luxury, but as a mark of God's blessing and presence. When joy disappears, it is a sign of misfortune; when it returns, it is a sign of restoration and hope. For the Christian, this means that seeking true joy — the kind that comes from God and honors Him — is part of the life of faith.

sens: To apply oil to something or someone
To consecrate someone to a function, especially royal or priestly, by anointing with oil
To mark an object with oil to make it a holy place
To anoint a body with perfume or oil
H4886.detail:
1. To anoint is primarily to pour or spread oil on the skin, clothing, or an object. It is a simple and concrete gesture: Isaiah 21:5 speaks of anointing the head, an image of the care one gives oneself.
2. But anointing becomes a sacred act when it has a religious significance: it is to consecrate someone or something to God. When the prophet Samuel anoints David in 1 Samuel 16:12-13, it is not just a cosmetic ointment; it is an act that marks David as the king chosen by God.
3. Anointing can also signify the investiture into a function: priests are anointed for the priesthood (Exodus 40:15), kings are anointed for royalty (1 Kings 1:39). The publicly poured oil signifies that God recognizes this person in their role.
4. Objects of worship are also anointed: Moses anoints the tabernacle and its utensils (Numbers 7:1) to sanctify them and set them apart for the service of God.
H4886.origine: The Hebrew verb mashach means to spread or rub, as one rubs oil on the skin. The image is that of a practical gesture that spreads a liquid over a surface. The word is linked to the economic and religious reality of Israel: oil was precious (used for lamps, cooking, body care, and rites), and its application marked something or someone as distinct and devoted to God. The corresponding Greek term in the Septuagint is aleiphô (to anoint) or sometimes chriô (to anoint sacramentally), depending on the context.
H4886.emploi: The verb anoint appears 66 times in the Old Testament. In the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), it refers to the anointing of the tabernacle and its utensils, as well as the anointing of the priests in Aaron (Exodus 40:9-15, Numbers 7:1). In the books of Kings and Samuel, anointing is the royal act par excellence: anointing of kings (Saul in 1 Samuel 10:1, David in 1 Samuel 16:13, Solomon in 1 Kings 1:39). These public anointing rites confer legitimacy and authority. Isaiah uses the verb for the mission of the Servant consecrated by God (Isaiah 61:1). Anointing always signifies a separation and a consecration: that which is anointed passes from the common to the sacred.
H4886.portee: For the Christian reader, the word anoint evokes total consecration to God. The anointing of the king or priest in Israel prefigures the Messiah, whose name itself means "the Anointed of the Lord." Understanding anointing means grasping that contact with holy oil marks a divine calling, a setting apart for a mission. For the believer's life, this reminds us that we are also anointed with the Spirit in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:21): we are consecrated and marked as belonging to God.

sens: Liquid fatty substance extracted from plants or animals
Product for consumption or offering in worship
H4887.detail:
1. Oil is a fatty and liquid substance, extracted notably from olives or other plants, used as food or fuel. In the two occurrences in the book of Ezra, it is listed among the food and material provisions necessary for the functioning of the temple: it was delivered to the priests along with wheat, wine, and salt for the burnt offerings and the maintenance of worship (Ezra 6:9 and 7:22).
2. Oil also has a cultic and religious dimension: it is a sacred product used in offerings at the temple and in the rites of Israelite worship. It symbolizes divine provision and the order established by God for the service of the temple.
H4887.origine: The Hebrew word מְשַׁח comes from a root that evokes anointing and oiliness. It literally designates oil as a concrete product. In the Old Testament, oil is inseparable from worship and daily life: it anoints kings and priests, it burns in the menorah of the sanctuary, it nourishes the people. It is a substance rich in religious symbolism in Israel.
H4887.emploi: The word מְשַׁח appears twice in the provided usages, both in the book of Ezra (6:9 and 7:22), during the reconstruction of the temple after the exile. In these two passages, oil is listed among the food and resources that the Persian authorities authorize to be delivered to the priests to ensure the regular functioning of worship. It is mentioned alongside wheat, wine, and salt — essential products for life and worship. The context is administrative and practical: it concerns the concrete supply of the temple. Oil is not here a detached symbol, but an indispensable material good.
H4887.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that God provides for the material needs of His people and the service rendered to Him. The listing of oil with other staple products shows that legitimate worship depends on concrete stewardship: faith is also expressed in the order of earthly things. It is a call to recognize divine providence in the details of daily life.

sens: Sacred oil prepared with spices, intended to consecrate people and objects of worship
The act of anointing someone with this oil, by which they are consecrated to God
Right, office, or dignity conferred by this consecration
Spiritual consecration and communion with God
H4888A.detail:
1. The anointing is primarily a specially prepared oil, mixed with precious spices according to a formula prescribed by God (Exodus 30:25). It is a concrete substance set apart for worship: it is used to anoint the tabernacle, the ark, and its utensils, in order to sanctify them and set them apart for God alone (Exodus 40:9).
2. The anointing also refers to the act of anointing: pouring this oil on someone's head, a ritual by which they are consecrated for the service of God. Aaron and his sons receive this anointing at their installation as priests (Leviticus 8:2 and 8:12), marking their entry into a sacred office.
3. The word can also refer to the right or portion that belongs to the anointed priest: it is a dignity, a charge offered by God to the one He has consecrated, as shown by the words addressed to the anointed priest (Leviticus 7:35).
4. Beyond the material rite, the anointing represents the transforming action of God that separates someone for His service and establishes them in an intimate relationship with Him — a consecration that touches the whole being.
H4888A.origine: The Hebrew word mishchah comes from the root mashach (to anoint), which evokes the action of pouring or rubbing oil on someone. Mashach is the basis of the word Mashiach (Messiah), literally "the anointed one," the one upon whom divine anointing has rested. All consecration to God in the Old Testament passes through this act of anointing with oil, a symbol of the presence and power of the Holy Spirit.
H4888A.emploi: The word mishchah appears 23 times in the laws of Leviticus and the book of Exodus, never in historical narratives. It primarily designates the anointing oil itself, a rare and reserved product, subject to the most precise prescriptions (a unique formula is prepared, Exodus 30:25, and its use is strictly regulated). It is the priest who bears the responsibility for it (Numbers 4:16). The usages show that the anointing applies to three categories: the objects of the sanctuary (tabernacle, altar, ark), the priests at the time of their inauguration, and by extension those who receive a divine consecration. The priestly context dominates: it always involves a ritual separation and setting apart for God.
H4888A.portee: The anointing teaches that our relationship with God does not rest on our merits or efforts, but on a divine action that sets us apart and transforms us. Just as oil spreads and permeates everything it touches, the anointing of the Holy Spirit (of which the material anointing was the sign) penetrates us entirely and consecrates us. It reminds the believer that they are set apart for God, called to a holy life, and that this dignity comes from the hand of the Lord alone.

sens: part reserved for God or His servants
portion of offering intended for worship
that which is set apart as sacred
H4888B.detail:
1. The consecrated portion is a part of a sacrifice or offering that God reserves for Himself or for His servants, the priests. It is a portion of a whole that is separated from the rest and declared holy, now belonging to the sacred domain. In Numbers 18:8, God speaks to Aaron about the consecrated portions of the offerings that the Israelites must give: it is a part that cannot be consumed by just anyone, but only by those who are ritually worthy.
2. The word also refers more broadly to any portion of offering set apart for divine worship, whether it be firstfruits, tithes, or other gifts. It conveys the idea of something that belongs to God and cannot be used for profane purposes without violating divine law.
H4888B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dip" or "to soak," likely in reference to anointing: the consecrated portions were often marked, anointed, or sprinkled to signify their separation and belonging to God. It is a term from the liturgical vocabulary of Leviticus and Numbers, used to speak of what is reserved for worship.
H4888B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 18:8, where God says to Aaron: "I give you charge of my consecrated portions." It is an instruction regarding the rights of the priests: they receive from God a special share of the offerings of the people, in compensation for their service at the tabernacle. The context is that of the Levitical law, which regulates the distribution of sacrifices between God, the priest, and sometimes the offerer.
H4888B.portee: This word reminds Christians that God demands a separation of the sacred and the profane, and that He desires to be honored by voluntary and regular gifts. It also illustrates the principle that those who serve God have the right to live from that service: it is a lesson in fairness towards pastors and workers of the Lord.

sens: Total annihilation, complete ruin of a person or thing
Death, extermination of living beings
Damage, devastation caused to a territory or community
Action or disposition to destroy, to annihilate
Net or trap that destroys
Figurative image of misfortune that engulfs
H4889.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes complete destruction, annihilation: in Exodus 12:13, the blood on the doors protects the Hebrews from the plague that would "destroy" the firstborn — it is the total ruin of a house that is avoided. 2. It applies to death and extermination: in Ezekiel 9:6, God commands to "destroy" the elderly, young men, and children, meaning to kill them mercilessly. 3. The word can also describe general damage, devastation: in Jeremiah 51:25, God calls Babylon a "mountain of destruction," she who has ravaged the whole earth through her conquests. 4. It sometimes denotes the very disposition to destroy: in Ezekiel 25:15, the Philistines "wanting to destroy everything" express their desire for total vengeance. 5. In Proverbs 18:9, one who is slack in work "destroys," meaning that they ruin their enterprise through laziness. 6. The word can also evoke a net or trap that captures and destroys: it is an object that annihilates.
H4889.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to break" or "to destroy." It is related to the concept of annihilation, reduction to nothing. Words of the same family express the action of destroying or the state of destruction. It is a common word in Hebrew to express not only physical ruin but also divine judgment and the eradication of evil.
H4889.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical and prophetic books. In Exodus 12:13, it denotes the destructive power that God stops. In Chronicles (2 Chronicles 20:23, 22:4), it expresses mutual extermination during wars. Jeremiah uses it to describe divine punishment on Babylon (51:25) and the traps of the wicked (5:26). Ezekiel often uses it for divine judgments: destruction of inhabitants, judgment on nations (9:6, 25:15). The word also appears in Proverbs for the ruin caused by laziness. Its meaning thus shifts from the concrete (to kill, to ravage) to the figurative (to ruin, to annihilate an enterprise), but always with the idea of irreversible and total damage.
H4889.portee: This word reminds us that destruction has real and serious consequences — whether it be divine judgment, human punishment, or ordinary ruin. It invites the believer to take sin and its fruits seriously, and to flee from malice and vengeance. It also shows that God can stop destruction and protect His own, as He did in Egypt: it is an invitation to trust and obedience.

sens: Moment of the day when the darkness of the night fades and the light of the sun begins to appear
First light of the day that rises
H4891.detail:
1. The dawn is the moment when the sun rises and brings forth the first lights on the horizon: it is this magical transition between the completely dark night and the clear day. In Psalm 110:3, dawn evokes the solemn moment when God gathers His people, as if this renewal were as magnificent and fresh as the birth of a new day.
2. It is also this first soft and nascent brightness that precedes the rising of the sun, when the sky begins to gradually illuminate. This image recalls both promise, renewal, and youth.
H4891.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "darkness" or "obscurity": dawn is literally the moment when darkness begins to dissipate. It is the contrast between the dark night and the nascent light that has given its name to this moment of the day.
H4891.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 110:3. In this royal and messianic psalm, dawn becomes an image of the youthful energy and vitality with which God's people gather around their king. It is a poetic, learned word that elevates the ordinary sense of morning into a symbol of renewed power.
H4891.portee: Dawn in this verse invites the believer to contemplate the eternal youth and endless energy that God gives to His people. It is an image of hope: just as each dawn brings new light after the night, God constantly renews the strength of those who follow Him.

sens: Annihilation, ruin of a city or a people
Instrument or means of destruction
The act of destroying, of annihilating
H4892.detail:
1. The word primarily designates complete destruction, the total ruin of a city or a people. It is the final state after devastation: what remains of a ravaged city. In Ezekiel 9:1, the angels tasked with punishing Jerusalem each hold "their instrument of destruction" in hand — it is the weapon or tool that causes this ruin.
2. The word can also refer to the process itself, the act of destroying: not just the result, but the action that leads to ruin. In this prophetic context, it is God's judgment in action, the execution of His sentence against sin.
3. By extension, it represents the misfortune, the disaster that falls upon a city: everything that reduces it to nothing, whether military, natural, or divine.
H4892.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root שׁחת (shachat), which means "to corrupt, to destroy, to spoil." The word mash.chet carries the idea of a progressive corruption that leads to total destruction: sin first corrupts, then it destroys. It is a process that moves from the inside to visible annihilation.
H4892.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 9:1. It describes the instrument used by the angels of judgment to strike Jerusalem. It is a grave term, reserved for the context of the execution of divine judgment. Its rarity underscores the solemnity of the moment: God specifically designates those who will bring ruin to His own city, showing that this destruction is not the result of chance, but a precise and ordered divine sentence.
H4892.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that God's judgment is neither capricious nor impulsive: it is executed by His angels, with formidable authority and precision. It invites repentance: destruction awaits those who persist in sin and rebellion against God. It also teaches us that God does not destroy without reason, but in response to the rejection of His warnings.

sens: Severe alteration of the face, transformation of facial appearance
State of deformation that provokes horror and dread in the observer
H4893A.detail:
1. The word designates a profound degradation of the face, a mutilation or deformation so severe that it renders the person unrecognizable. In Isaiah 52:14, it describes how the face of the suffering Servant was ravaged: "So marred was His visage, more than any man, and His form more than the sons of men." It is the extreme physical culmination of inflicted suffering.
2. This disfigurement provokes "dismay" — a feeling of rejection and horror mixed before such a spectacle. The word emphasizes not only the physical damage but the emotional effect it produces: one turns away, seized with dread at seeing this unrecognizable man.
H4893A.origine: The Hebrew word derives from a root evoking the idea of corruption, alteration, or ruin. It is rare in the Bible and used precisely when one wants to evoke an irreversible deformation — not a temporary wound, but a change so radical that it removes from the person their visible identity. Its use in Isaiah 52 concerning the suffering Servant makes it a term loaded with prophetic significance.
H4893A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 52:14, at the heart of the song of the suffering Servant. There, it describes the physical sufferings of the Messiah before His resurrection. The context shows that this disfigurement is not a mere accident: it is linked to condemnation, to the blows received, to the path to the cross. This rare and strong word marks a turning point in the prophetic understanding of what the Messiah would endure for salvation.
H4893A.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the price Jesus paid for our salvation — not only in inner pain but also in physical and visible humiliation. Isaiah 52:14 invites us to contemplate what the Servant suffered and to recognize its significance: His extreme humiliation is the means of our redemption. This passage helps the believer not to turn away from the suffering of Christ, but to see in it the proof of His love.

sens: Physical defect, injury, or malformation of an animal
Alteration or corruption of a sacrificial victim that renders it unfit for worship
Imperfection that disqualifies an offering
H4893B.detail:
1. Physical defect, injury, or malformation of an animal: this is a visible lesion on the body of a beast, a wound, or an absence of a body part. In Leviticus 22:25, a "mutilated" victim does not have the required physical integrity.
2. Alteration of a sacrificial victim: the word specifically refers to corruption, defilement, or damage that renders an offering unfit for the service of God. This is a concept from Israel's ritual — a mutilated victim cannot be offered as a sacrifice, as it is considered unworthy to be presented before the Lord.
3. Disqualifying imperfection: beyond the simple physical defect, there is the idea that this alteration signifies a moral or ritual unworthiness. What God receives must be whole, healthy, blameless — mutilation symbolizes anything that obstructs a right relationship with the Lord.
H4893B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of defect or damage. Its context is that of the Levitical ritual, where the purity and integrity of the victim are essential. The law of Moses repeated this requirement to ensure that offerings to God meet the highest standards.
H4893B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 22:25. It occurs in a list of precise rules regarding acceptable victims for sacrifice. The law prohibits the offering of mutilated or defective animals, showing that Israel was to offer its best. This requirement reflects the holy character of God and the respect due to divine worship.
H4893B.portee: This word reminds us of a spiritual truth: God is not satisfied with superficial sacrifices or leftovers. He demands the whole heart, sincere commitment, the best part of our lives. The notion of mutilation challenges us about what we present to God — are our offerings, our vows, our service integral and true, or are there defects within us that we hide?

sens: place where nets are spread to dry
flat and clear surface
H4894A.detail:
1. The word specifically refers to a place where fishermen spread their nets after fishing to dry or repair them. In Ezekiel 26:5 and 26:14, the ruin of Tyre is described as becoming "a place where nets are spread" — the proud port city will be reduced to a bare and clear surface, just suitable for fishermen to spread their nets. It is an image of total degradation, from a destroyed temple to the most humble utility.
2. The word can also more broadly evoke a flat and clear surface, suitable for receiving something that is spread out. This image conveys the idea of lowering: from splendor to everyday use.
H4894A.origine: The word comes from the root שׁטח (shataḥ), which means "to spread," "to deploy" (as one spreads a garment or cloth). The term מִשְׁטָח retains this concrete idea of the action of spreading. The root belongs to the common vocabulary of Hebrew for all gestures of extension and spreading. This image of something spread out on the ground, laid flat, perfectly fits the prophetic description of the fall of a great city.
H4894A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Ezekiel 26, in the Lord's discourse against Tyre. The prophet announces that this magnificent, proud, and trading city will be destroyed and delivered to the nations to become "a place where nets are spread." This repetition (verses 5 and 14) reinforces the effect of humiliation: the contrast between past greatness and future degradation is at its maximum. The context is always that of the ruin of a powerful city.
H4894A.portee: This image of the "place of spreading" speaks to the reader about the fragility of human power and the pride of the world. It reminds us that God humbles the proud and that even the most brilliant commercial splendor can be reduced to nothing. The choice of such a humble image — the surface where nets dry — underscores the total reduction of prestige and power.

sens: place where something is spread to dry or prepare
designated surface for laying out fishing nets
H4894B.detail:
1. The word specifically designates a place reserved for the action of spreading a material or object to dry, prepare, or treat it. It is a workspace where something is laid out flat.
2. In the unique biblical context of fish and fishing, it refers to the place where fishermen lay and spread their nets before or after fishing. In Ezekiel 47:10, "they will spread the nets" evokes these spaces by the water where fishermen work: the nets must be spread to be inspected, repaired, or dried.
H4894B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to spread" or "to deploy." It is a nominal form that designates not the action itself, but the place where this action regularly takes place. The root evokes the idea of laying flat, deploying a surface.
H4894B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 47:10. The prophet describes the vision of a miraculous river flowing from the temple, whose waters bring life to the desert of the Dead Sea. He paints a picture of restoration where fishermen will finally be able to exercise their trade abundantly, with nets to spread on the banks. The context is one of regeneration and hope: this place of spreading symbolizes the return of life and normal human activity in a barren region.
H4894B.portee: This verse reminds us that God promises not only the salvation of the soul but also the concrete restoration of life on earth — work, prosperity, restored nature. The image of the spread net speaks to those who work with their hands: God sees and values ordinary labor, and He will restore it in His Kingdom.

sens: Open hostility, declared conflict between enemies
State of revolt against an authority
Hostile opposition to God and His plan
H4895.detail:
1. Rebellion is an active and manifest hostility, a state of declared enemy: it is being in open conflict. In Hosea 9:8, Ephraim is described as an "enemy in the house of his God," meaning someone who actively opposes God instead of obeying Him.
2. The word also expresses revolt against an authority: refusing submission and allegiance. In Hosea 9:7, the prophet speaks of "the greatness of your iniquities and your rebellions," showing that Israel has voluntarily risen up against the Lord.
3. More precisely, it is the hostile opposition directed against God Himself: not merely human enmity, but the posture of one who rejects the Lord and refuses His authority.
H4895.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising up against, opposing forcefully. It is related to verbs meaning "to hate" and "to fight." What characterizes rebellion is that it is always directed: one does not experience it passively, one commits it actively against someone.
H4895.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Hosea 9. In these two verses, it characterizes Israel's position before God: the people have committed iniquity and refuse to submit. Rebellion is linked to spiritual blindness (the prophet "is delirious") and to hostility toward God instead of walking with Him. It is a strong word, which does not denote a mere momentary disobedience, but a state of declared and persistent opposition.
H4895.portee: Rebellion is not just a fault among others: it is taking a stand against God Himself. This word challenges the believer about the difference between a fault committed and a heart that intentionally rises up against the Lord. It invites us to examine whether our walk with God is a sincere submission or a hidden rebellion.

sens: Established order, law that governs something
Power to impose that order, authority
H4896.detail:
1. A "rule" is an established order, a law that structures and governs something — here, the heavenly laws that regulate the movement of the stars and the phenomena of the sky. In Job 38:33, God asks Job if he knows "the rules of the heavens," meaning the invisible laws that order the universe and keep everything in place.
2. The word also refers to the "power" or "authority" to impose and enforce that order. When one "rules" according to a rule, one exercises dominion based on an established order — this is the natural meaning of the verb "to reign" or "to command" that follows from it.
H4896.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "tracing," "marking," and by extension, "establishing an order" or a "line of conduct." The word belongs to the family of terms that express organization, structure, and governance. It is a technical term that designates less a written rule than a principle of order that manifests in action: a rule that "functions," that "governs."
H4896.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 38:33, at the heart of the discourse where God questions Job about his limitations. God asks Job about his understanding of the laws that govern the heavens and whether he can exercise his authority on earth — thus raising the question of who truly holds power and knowledge of the cosmic order. The usage is highly poetic and theological: it is less about an administrative "rule" than about a principle of divine order that escapes human understanding.
H4896.portee: This word reminds us that behind the universe and its phenomena exists an order established by God, a wisdom and governance that infinitely surpasses us. It invites humility in the face of the divine mystery: we grasp very little of the rules that order the world. Recognizing these rules and this divine authority is to accept our place in a universe governed by a wisdom far beyond our capabilities.

sens: Fine and precious fabric made from silk worm fibers, shiny in color
Luxury clothing or ornament reserved for high-ranking individuals
H4897.detail:
1. Silk is a very fine, smooth, and shiny fabric, of great softness, obtained by weaving fibers produced by silk worms. It is a rare and costly material, highly prized in the ancient world for the beauty and prestige it confers on the wearer. The prophet Ezekiel describes silk as one of the noblest garments with which God adorns Jerusalem, symbolizing the wealth and glory He grants her (Ezekiel 16:10).
2. By extension, silk refers to any clothing or ornament made from this precious fabric. It symbolizes luxury, royalty, and social distinction. In Ezekiel 16:13, silk appears among the signs of beauty and splendor of a queen, alongside gold, silver, and fine linen, emphasizing that the one who wears silk enjoys a high status and great wealth.
H4897.origine: The Hebrew word מֶשִׁי (méshi) specifically designates silk, a rare imported material in ancient Israel. The exact etymology is uncertain, but the word may be related to Semitic roots expressing the fineness or softness of the fabric. Due to the cost and rarity of silk, this word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of great wealth and royal luxury.
H4897.emploi: The word silk (Heb. méshi) appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 16 of the book of Ezekiel. These two occurrences describe the luxurious garments with which the Lord adorns Jerusalem to make her a queen. In Ezekiel 16:10, silk is mentioned alongside embroidered fine linen and blue-dyed shoes, as part of the royal attire offered to the city. In Ezekiel 16:13, it reappears in the enumeration of the riches and ornaments that testify to the beauty and perfection of Jerusalem made queen. The context is always one of material splendor and prestige, reflecting divine generosity and the promises of exaltation made to Jerusalem.
H4897.portee: Silk in these passages symbolizes God's generosity and goodness toward His people. It reminds us that God desires not only to provide for essential needs but also to beautify and honor His people by granting them beauty and dignity. For the Christian reader, silk also evokes how God wishes to cover with glory and purity those He loves, an image of the transformation that the Gospel brings to those who receive it.

sens: Man of Judah during the time of exile and return, father of Berekiah
H4898G.detail: Meshazabeel is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:4. He is the father of Berekiah, who was the father of Meshullam. The latter participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile. Although little known, Meshazabeel belongs to a family of builders and servants of the restoration project of Jerusalem.
H4898G.origine: The name Meshazabeel means "God delivers" or "God saves" in Hebrew. It is composed of elements expressing the divine action of salvation and protection. This name reflects a trust in God, characteristic of the names given to the people returning from Babylonian exile.
H4898G.emploi: Meshazabeel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:4. He is mentioned as the father of Berekiah and the grandfather of Meshullam, who engaged in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. Although few details are given about his personal life, his genealogical position reveals a family involved in the restoration and rebuilding efforts of the Judean people.

sens: Name of a man during the Exile and Return
Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H4898H.detail: Meshazabeel is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile. His name means "God delivers," which expresses trust in divine deliverance. He appears among the leaders of the people who affixed their seal to the solemn covenant that Nehemiah made with Israel, thus showing their commitment to observe God's Law after the reconstruction of the Temple and Jerusalem.
H4898H.origine: The Hebrew name Meshazabeel is composed of two parts: "God" (El) and a verb meaning "to deliver" or "to save." It is a typical theophoric name, that is, a name borne in the Old Testament to confess that God is the one who saves and protects His people.
H4898H.emploi: Meshazabeel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:21. He is presented as one of the leaders of the people who participated in the solemn ceremony of sealing the covenant shortly after the return from exile in Babylon. This unique mention shows that he was an important figure among the leaders of Israel at this critical time of reconstruction of the people and renewal of their commitment to God.

sens: Man of the period of exile and return to Jerusalem
H4898I.detail: Meschézabeel is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the people of Israel return from captivity in Babylon. His name means "God delivers" in Hebrew. He is the father of Pethachja, who held an important position with the king to manage the affairs of the people (Nehemiah 11:24). Meschézabeel is a descendant of Zerah, son of Judah, which connects him to a prestigious genealogical line of the tribe of Judah.
H4898I.origine: The name Meschézabeel is composed of the Hebrew "meschah" (to deliver, to save) and "el" (God). It expresses the idea that God saves or delivers. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the Hebrews to express their faith in divine salvific action.
H4898I.emploi: Meschézabeel is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 11:24. He appears in the context of the return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. His main role is to be the father of Pethachja, a commissioner of the king in charge of the affairs of the people. He is identified as a descendant of Zerah, son of Judah, which emphasizes his connection to the genealogy of Judah and his importance in the restoration of the Israelite community.
H4898I.portee: The name Meschézabeel, "God delivers," reminds the reader that the return from exile is an act of divine deliverance. The presence of characters like him and his son Pethachja in the reconstruction shows how God, throughout history, prepares and raises faithful men to restore His people. It is an invitation to recognize the hidden yet certain action of God in our circumstances.

sens: Person consecrated by a holy anointing with oil
The high priest of Israel
The king of Israel
Announced messianic figure, the Christ
H4899.detail:
1. The anointing with oil was a gesture of consecration: oil was poured on a person's head to set them apart for God and entrust them with a sacred mission. It is a visible act that marked divine intervention. King David speaks of "the Lord's anointed" in this way, showing that this anointing was the seal of God Himself (1 Samuel 26:11).
2. The high priest received the anointing and was called "the anointed priest": it separated him from other priests and made him responsible before God for the sins of the people (Leviticus 4:3).
3. The king of Israel was anointed to reign in God's name. David, Saul, and their successors were "the Lord's anointed," which meant they governed by divine authority and that attacking them was to attack God's plan (2 Samuel 1:14).
4. The term "Messiah" (anointed) refers to the one whom God would promise to save His people. The prophets announced a final anointed one, a messianic prince, of whom Jesus is the fulfillment. The prophet Daniel speaks of "the Messiah, the prince" (Daniel 9:25).
H4899.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "mashach" which means "to anoint with oil, to rub." Anointing was a common practice in Israel to consecrate kings, priests, and sometimes prophets. It was a public and tangible sign that God chose this person and invested them with His Spirit. The word "Messiah" in French comes directly from this Hebrew "mashiach" (the anointed one), and the Greek "christos" translates this same concept: all three fundamentally mean "the one who has been anointed."
H4899.emploi: This word appears 38 times in the Old Testament. It primarily refers to the kings of Judah: Saul, David, and his descendants. Psalm 18:51 asks God to have mercy on "His anointed," meaning the reigning king. It also applies to the high priest, particularly in the laws of Leviticus concerning sin offerings. It is also found regarding Cyrus, the Persian king, whom God calls "anointed" because he frees the exiles. Gradually, the term takes on an eschatological significance (concerning the end times): the prophets speak of a coming Messiah, a final anointed one sent by God. This messianic expectation structures all of Israel's hope and culminates in the New Testament, where Jesus is recognized as the Messiah, the Christ.
H4899.portee: This word reminds us that God chooses instruments to accomplish His plan: kings, priests, prophets. But it points especially to Jesus, the anointed one par excellence, to whom all other anointings foreshadowed. Understanding the meaning of the word "Messiah" helps the Christian grasp who Jesus is: the one in whom all of God's promises are concentrated, the definitive king and priest, invested with the divine Spirit for the salvation of humanity.
